label: like, as (similarity)
meaning_en: A particle that attaches to a noun and means “like N, as N is”. It makes a comparison of quality or manner, and in a few time-noun collocations it adds the sense of “without fail” or “very early”.
usage: It attaches directly to a noun, without a space: “얼음같이 차갑다”. The predicate is usually an adjective or a verb that describes what the noun is like. Do not mix it up with the adverb “같이” (together), which follows “N와/과” and takes a space. Fixed collocations: “매일같이” (every single day), “새벽같이” (at the crack of dawn), “철석같이 믿다” (to trust unshakably).

examples.en: That person is as kind-hearted as an angel.

examples.ko: 네 손이 얼음같이 차가워서 깜짝 놀랐어.
examples.en: Your hands are as cold as ice, so I was startled.
Minjun goes to the library every single day.

examples.ko: 지수는 새벽같이 일어나 출근 준비를 했다.
examples.en: Jisu got up at the crack of dawn and got ready for work.
The trip passed by like a dream.

compare.difference: In similes “같이” and “처럼” are near-synonyms and can usually replace each other. The time-noun collocations (“매일같이”, “새벽같이”) are the set phrases of “같이”.

pair.en: That person is as kind as an angel.
That person is as kind as an angel.

compare.difference: The adverb “같이” (together) is a different word from the particle: it follows “N와/과” and means “in company with”. The particle only compares.

pair.en: The teacher is as easy to be around as a friend.
I watched a movie together with my friend.

pitfalls.note: Attached to a noun, it means “like”, not “together with”. For “together”, use “N와/과 같이”.
pitfalls.en: I watched a movie together with my friend.

topik_tip: The time-noun phrases “매일같이” and “새벽같이” are worth knowing as units: they are adverbs meaning “every single day” and “at the crack of dawn”, not similes.

label: listing every item, “X and Y and all”
meaning_en: A particle that is repeated on each noun in a list, “N이고 N이고 (다)”, and says that all of them are included: “be it A or B, all of it”. The sentence usually ends with a summing-up word such as “다” or “모두”.
usage: After a noun ending in a consonant it is “이고” (“밥이고”, “서울이고”); after a vowel the “이” drops (“커피고”, “차고”). It goes on every item, including the last, and the main clause normally sums up with “다/모두/전부” or makes a sweeping statement. Typical collocations: “낮이고 밤이고” (day and night), “이고 저고” (this and that). It is a spoken, slightly emphatic way of listing.

examples.en: The rice, the bread, everything looks delicious.
Minjun did nothing but work, day and night.

examples.ko: 서울이고 부산이고 주말에는 어디나 사람이 많다.
examples.en: Be it Seoul or Busan, there are crowds everywhere on weekends.

examples.ko: 요즘은 영화고 드라마고 볼 시간이 없어요.
examples.en: These days I have no time to watch movies, dramas, or anything.

examples.ko: 한국어는 문법이고 어휘고 하나도 쉬운 게 없다.
examples.en: In Korean, neither grammar nor vocabulary is easy at all.

compare.difference: “N이고 N이고” lists the items and covers all of them. “N이든 N이든” says it makes no difference which one: any of them will do.

pair.en: I eat fruit, vegetables, everything well.
Fruit or vegetables, give me whichever.

compare.difference: “하고” and “와/과” are the plain “and”. “이고” is not a plain “and”: it needs the repeated pattern and a sweeping main clause.

pair.en: I bought apples, pears, the lot.
I bought apples and pears.

pitfalls.note: The particle goes on every item, including the last. With only the first item marked, the list breaks off.
pitfalls.en: I ate the rice, the bread, all of it.

pitfalls.note: It is not a plain “and”. A simple list of two things takes “하고” or “와/과”.
pitfalls.en: I bought apples, pears, the lot.

topik_tip: Look for the pair “N이고 N이고” followed by “다/모두”. It reads as “all of them, no matter which”, similar in effect to “N이든 N이든 다”.

label: as, according to
meaning_en: A particle meaning “as N, in line with N”: the action or state follows the noun exactly. It is also used with a noun to say that each thing goes its own way (“제멋대로”, “각자 마음대로”).
usage: It attaches to a noun without a space: “계획대로”, “예상대로”, “약속대로”, “법대로”, “말씀대로”. After a verb or adjective modifier the same word is a dependent noun and is written with a space (“말한 대로”, “본 대로”). Common collocations: “예상대로” (as expected), “마음대로” (as one pleases), “순서대로” (in order).

examples.en: Everything went as planned.
As expected, the result was not good.
As promised, lunch is on me today.
I did as the teacher said, and the problem got solved.
Please handle it according to the law.

compare.difference: “말씀대로” (noun) and “말씀하신 대로” (verb form) mean the same. The first attaches to the noun, the second is a modifier plus a spaced word.

pair.en: I will do as you say.
I will do as you said.

compare.difference: “법대로” is plain and direct. “법에 따라” is the more formal, document-like way of saying “in accordance with the law”.

pair.en: We will handle it according to the law.
We will handle it in accordance with the law.

pitfalls.note: After a verb it is a separate word: write a space. Only after a noun is it attached.
pitfalls.en: I did as I said.

topik_tip: Spacing is the usual test item: “N대로” is attached, but “-은/는 대로” after a verb or adjective is spaced.

label: from (a source or starting point)
meaning_en: A formal particle marking the source or origin of something: the person or place something comes from, the one who sends, gives or causes it. It translates as “from”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “로부터” (“친구로부터”, “서울로부터”); after any other consonant it is “으로부터” (“집으로부터”, “사람으로부터”). It marks givers and senders (“받다, 듣다, 배우다”), sources (“들어오다”), and what one is freed or protected from (“벗어나다, 보호하다, 자유롭다”). It is written and formal; speech prefers “한테서/에게서” for people and “에서” for places.

examples.en: Yesterday I received a letter from an old friend.
This system was brought in from Japan.
We came to receive subsidy money from the government.
We must protect children from danger.

examples.ko: 학교는 역으로부터 걸어서 오 분 거리에 있다.
examples.en: The school is a five-minute walk from the station.

compare.difference: For a person as the source, “에게서” is the everyday choice and “으로부터” the written, formal one. The meaning is the same.

pair.en: I received a present from a friend.
I received a present from a friend.

compare.difference: For a place as a starting point, “에서” is the everyday particle; “으로부터” sounds more formal and is also used for time and distance.

pair.en: It is five minutes from the station.
It is five minutes from the station.

pitfalls.note: A noun ending in ㄹ takes “로부터”, never “으로부터”.
pitfalls.en: A letter came from Seoul.

pitfalls.note: It marks the source or giver, not the one who receives. The recipient takes “에게”.
pitfalls.en: I gave a present to a friend.

topik_tip: In 읽기 passages “으로부터” is found with verbs of receiving and release: “받다, 듣다, 벗어나다, 보호하다”.

label: as much as (degree)
meaning_en: A particle that attaches to a noun and means “to the same degree as N”: it compares extent, amount or level. In a negative sentence it means “not as ... as N”.
usage: It attaches to a noun or pronoun without a space: “너만큼”, “작년만큼”, “기대만큼”. The predicate expresses a degree (an adjective such as “크다” or a verb like “좋아하다”). With a negative it says that N is the higher standard (“작년만큼 덥지 않다”). “만큼은” singles out one thing for emphasis: “이번만큼은” (this time, at least), “이것만큼은”. The dependent noun “-ㄴ/는 만큼” after a verb is spaced and is a different row.

examples.en: Minjun is as tall as Jisu.
This year is not as hot as last year.

examples.ko: 나만큼 너를 아끼는 사람은 없을 거야.
examples.en: No one cares for you as much as I do.
The exam result was not as good as expected.
This time, I will keep my promise for sure.

compare.difference: “만큼” compares degree, “처럼” compares manner or likeness. The minimal pair differs in what is being matched.

pair.en: I want to sing as well as you do.
I want to sing like you.

compare.difference: “만큼” says two things are equal; “보다” says one is more than the other.

pair.en: They run as fast as Jisu.
They run faster than Jisu.

pitfalls.note: “만큼” matches degree. For manner or resemblance, use “처럼”.
pitfalls.en: I want to fly like a bird.

pitfalls.note: After a verb form it is a separate word with a space; only a noun takes it attached.
pitfalls.en: You get as much as you put in effort.

topik_tip: “N만큼 + negative” (“not as ... as N”) and “이번만큼은” (this time, at least) are the two shapes to recognise in exams.

label: to/at a person (speech, reaction)
meaning_en: A colloquial particle that marks the person a speech act or a reaction is aimed at, like “에게/한테” but limited to verbs such as “말하다, 시키다, 웃다, 화내다, 욕하다”. Typical shape: “나보고 ...(으)라고 하다” (they told me to ...).
usage: It attaches to person nouns and pronouns (“나보고, 너보고, 민준이보고”) and is heard in speech and informal writing. It is almost always followed by a verb of saying, commanding or reacting, often with a quoted clause: “나보고 가라고 했다”. It is not used with verbs of giving or receiving: those need “에게/한테”. The set phrase “나보고 어쩌라고?” means “What do you want me to do?”. Do not confuse it with “보고” from the verb “보다”.

examples.ko: 엄마가 나보고 방 좀 치우라고 했다.
examples.en: Mom told me to clean my room.
The teacher told Minjun to stand up.
People say I am diligent.

examples.ko: 승규는 아무 이유 없이 나보고 화를 냈다.
examples.en: Seunggyu got angry at me for no reason.
What is everyone expecting me to do?

compare.difference: With speech verbs “보고” and “한테” mean the same, and “한테” is the neutral, safer form. “보고” is only spoken-style and only with some verbs.

pair.en: Minjun told me to go.
Minjun told me to go.

pitfalls.note: “보고” does not go with verbs of giving or receiving; those take “한테/에게”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my friend a book.

topik_tip: In reading dialogues the shape “N보고 ...라고 하다” is the same as “N한테 ...라고 하다”: read it as “told N to ...”.

label: only, nothing but
meaning_en: A particle meaning “only N, nothing other than N”. It typically closes the sentence with “이다” (“너뿐이야”) or appears in “N뿐만 아니라” (not only N but also).
usage: It attaches to a noun without a space and then needs “이다” (“너뿐이다”), “뿐이 아니다” or “뿐(만) 아니라”. It does not combine freely with an ordinary verb: for “only eat bread” use “만” (“빵만 먹었다”). After a verb modifier “뿐” is a dependent noun and is spaced (“웃을 뿐이다”, I can only laugh). Common phrases: “하나뿐” (the only one), “뿐만 아니라” (not only ... but also).

examples.en: You are the only one I can trust.
There was nothing in the room but one old chair.

examples.ko: 그 가수는 노래뿐만 아니라 춤도 잘 춘다.
examples.en: Besides singing, that singer also dances well.

examples.ko: 이 일을 할 수 있는 사람은 지수뿐입니다.
examples.en: Jisu is the only person who can do this job.
All that remains is regret.

compare.difference: “만” attaches to any word and works with any predicate. “뿐” closes the sentence with “이다” and sounds more final.

pair.en: I trust only you.
The only person I trust is you.

compare.difference: “뿐이다” and “밖에 없다” are near-synonyms for “nothing but”. “뿐” ends in “이다”, “밖에” always needs a negative.

pair.en: You are the only one I can trust.
There is no one I can trust but you.

pitfalls.note: With an ordinary verb the particle for “only” is “만”; “뿐” needs “이다” or “뿐 아니라”.
pitfalls.en: I ate only bread.

pitfalls.note: After a verb form it is spaced as a dependent noun.
pitfalls.en: All I could do was laugh.

topik_tip: “뿐만 아니라 ... 도” is the standard “not only ... but also” frame in 읽기.

label: calling a person (vocative)
meaning_en: The vocative particle “아/야” attached to a name or a noun when calling or addressing someone close or younger: “민준아, 이리 와.”
usage: After a consonant-final name it is “아” (“민준아, 유민아, 지영아”), after a vowel-final name “야” (“지수야, 승규야, 영수야”). It is used to friends, younger people, children and also to animals and things in poems and songs (“달아”). It is intimate speech (“해체” or “해라체” sentences follow it) and is not used to someone you must show respect to: with elders you use the title alone (“선생님, ...”) and with polite adults “씨”. Common: “얘들아” (hey, kids).

examples.en: Minjun, have you eaten?
Jisu, come over here for a moment.
Yumin, what time is the exam tomorrow?
Seunggyu, it has been a while. Have you been well?
Kids, be quiet.
Moon, you are shining bright again today.

compare.difference: “아/야” is for close friends and juniors; “씨” is the neutral, polite way to address an adult you are not close to.

pair.en: Jisu, where are you going?
Jisu, where are you going?

pitfalls.note: After a consonant-final name the particle is “아”, not “야”.
pitfalls.en: Minjun, come here.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel-final name it is “야”, not “아”.
pitfalls.en: Jisu, what are you doing?

topik_tip: Pick the form from the last sound of the name: consonant gives “아”, vowel gives “야”.

label: polite “요” on words and phrases
meaning_en: A particle that adds politeness to a word, phrase or clause ending, turning intimate speech (“해체”) into the soft polite “해요체”: “저기요”, “빨리요”, “그래서요?”.
usage: It attaches to nouns, adverbs and the ends of clauses, whether or not a full ending follows (“물 좀요”, “지금 바로요?”, “그런데요”, “그래서요?”). That is why it appears on fragments and in the middle of sentences: “저는요, 어제요, ...”. In conversation “여기요” and “저기요” are the standard ways to call a waiter or stranger. It does not stack onto “합쇼체” endings (“-습니다”).

examples.en: Excuse me, could we get some water here?
As for me, I am going to the library.
And then? What happened next?

examples.ko: 지금 바로요? 아직 준비가 안 됐는데요.
examples.en: Right now? I am not ready yet.
Two coffees here, please.

compare.difference: The particle “요” gives soft, conversational politeness (“해요체”); “-습니다” is the formal “합쇼체” used in speeches, announcements and business.

pair.en: Are you going now?
Are you going now?

pitfalls.note: Do not add “요” to a “합쇼체” ending. Choose the “해요체” ending instead.
pitfalls.en: Thank you.

pitfalls.note: A bare noun with “요” works as an answer fragment, but a full statement needs the copula “이에요”.
pitfalls.en: I am a student.

topik_tip: In listening items, “요” on a fragment or after a pause marks “해요체” speech: it is polite, not a different meaning.

label: quoting directly, “called ...”
meaning_en: A quotation particle: “라고” follows a directly quoted word or sentence, and “이라고” follows a consonant-final noun being named or quoted. “N(이)라고 하다” means “to be called N”.
usage: In a direct quote it attaches to the quoted words (“‘가자’라고 말했다”). With a noun it is “이라고” after a consonant (“한글이라고”) and “라고” after a vowel (“김치라고”). It combines with “하다, 말하다, 부르다, 외치다, 소리치다, 쓰다”. The collocation “(이)라고 해서” means “just because it is ...”. For indirect quotes the endings “-다고/-라고” are used instead.

examples.en: In Korean this food is called “비빔밥”.
The teacher said, “Hand in your homework by tomorrow.”
My friend calls me a “genius”.
The child came running, shouting “Mom!”

examples.ko: 부자라고 해서 다 행복한 것은 아니다.
examples.en: Just because people are rich does not mean they are all happy.

compare.difference: “라고” repeats the words as spoken (direct quote). “-다고” reports them from the speaker’s own point of view (indirect quote), so the sentence form changes.

pair.en: I said, “I'm hungry.”
I said that I was hungry.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel-final noun there is no “이”: it is “라고”.
pitfalls.en: This is called kimchi.

pitfalls.note: After a consonant-final noun “이” is needed.
pitfalls.en: This letter system is called “한글”.

topik_tip: Telling direct (“라고”) from indirect (“-다고”) quotation is a typical grammar question; in direct quotes the quoted words stay unchanged.

label: past cut off from the present
meaning_en: A doubled past marker that presents an event or state as finished and no longer connected to the present: “I used to ...”, “there was a time when ...”. It often hints that the situation has since changed.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and to “이다”: “가다 → 갔었다”, “먹다 → 먹었었다”, “살다 → 살았었다”, “하다 → 했었다”. It sets the situation apart from now, so it pairs with time words such as “예전에, 전에, 어릴 때, 한때, 그때”, and it is often followed by a contrast with the present (“-었었는데 지금은 ...”). If a result still holds, or the event is recent, plain “-었-” is used. In speech it is common with “-었었어요” in the “해요체”.

examples.en: I used to live in the countryside when I was little.
I used to smoke, but I have quit now.

examples.ko: 그 가게는 전에 여기에 있었었는데 이사 갔나 봐요.
examples.en: That shop used to be here, but it seems to have moved.
I, too, played the guitar for a while once.
This road used to be very narrow.

compare.difference: Plain “-었-” just reports a past event. “-었었-” adds that it is over and no longer true now.

pair.en: I lived in Seoul last year.
I used to live in Seoul last year.

compare.difference: “-은 적이 있다” says one has had the experience. “-었었-” says the event happened in the past and is over, without focusing on experience.

pair.en: I have been to Jeju Island.
I went to Jeju Island.

pitfalls.note: It marks a situation that is no longer true, so it does not fit a state that continues now.
pitfalls.right: 저는 어릴 때 이 동네에 살았었어요.
pitfalls.en: I used to live in this neighborhood when I was little.

topik_tip: In reading passages, “-었었-” plus “지금은” signals a contrast between a past situation and the present.

label: if, once (condition)
meaning_en: A connective ending meaning “if it is the case that ...” or “once it turns out that ...”. It sets a condition that may come true, and the main clause is normally a command, request, suggestion or promise.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems: “도착하다 → 도착하거든”, “좋다 → 좋거든”, “학생이다 → 학생이거든”; it can follow “-었-” (“끝났거든”). The main clause is an order, request or invitation (“-아라/-세요/-자”) or a promise, rarely a plain statement of fact: for “비가 오면 길이 막힌다” use “-으면”. The sentence-final “-거든(요)” (giving a reason) is a different row, “-거든2”.

examples.en: Call me when you get home.
Once the exam date is set, let's study together.
If a word you do not know comes up, look it up in a dictionary.
If you like it, take it.
If it is hard, tell me at any time.

compare.difference: With a command or a proposal as the main clause the two are near-synonyms. “-으면” also handles plain statements, habits and general truths; “-거든” does not.

pair.en: Once the rain stops, let's set off.
When the rain stops, the roads get jammed.

compare.difference: “-거든2” closes a sentence and gives a reason (“I'm hungry, I skipped breakfast, see”). “-거든1” is a conditional that continues into a main clause.

pair.en: If you are hungry, eat first.
I'm hungry. I did not eat breakfast, you see.

pitfalls.note: The main clause needs to be a command, request, suggestion or promise, not a statement of fact.
pitfalls.en: If it rains, use an umbrella.

topik_tip: “-거든” followed by an imperative (“-아라/-세요”) or “-자” is the condition ending; when the clause closes the sentence, it is “-거든2”.

label: listing examples, “things like X or Y”
meaning_en: A connective ending that lists actions or states as examples, usually followed by “하다”: “X도 한다거나 Y도 한다거나 하다” means “do things like X or Y”. It is a contraction of “-는다고 하거나”.
usage: Verbs take “-ㄴ다거나/-는다거나” (“가다 → 간다거나”, “먹다 → 먹는다거나”, “놀다 → 논다거나”, “보다 → 본다거나”); adjectives take “-다거나” (“피곤하다거나”); nouns take “-(이)라거나” (“학생이라거나”); commands and suggestions take “-(으)라거나, -자거나”. It is normally repeated at least twice, and the example list ends with “하다” or a sweeping noun such as “일”. It is conversational and a little vague on purpose.

examples.ko: 주말에는 영화를 본다거나 산책을 한다거나 해요.
examples.en: On weekends I do things like watching a movie or going for a walk.

examples.ko: 민준이는 피곤하다거나 힘들다거나 하는 말을 절대 하지 않는다.
examples.en: Minjun never says things like being tired or finding things hard.

examples.ko: 비가 온다거나 눈이 온다거나 해도 약속은 지켜야 한다.
examples.en: Even if it rains or snows or something, a promise has to be kept.

examples.ko: 스트레스를 받을 때는 음악을 듣는다거나 운동을 한다거나 하면 도움이 된다.
examples.en: When you are stressed, things like listening to music or exercising help.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 학생이라거나 직장인이라거나 하는 정보는 없었다.
examples.en: There was no information such as whether that person was a student or an office worker.

compare.difference: “-거나” offers two alternatives (“A or B”). “-는다거나 ... 하다” gives examples among others, so the list is open.

pair.en: I read a book or watch a movie.
I do things like reading or watching movies.

compare.difference: “-기도 하고 ... -기도 하다” is a close alternative that says the speaker does each of these things as well. The two are near-synonyms.

pair.ko: 책을 읽기도 하고 영화를 보기도 해요.
pair.en: I read books and also watch movies.
I do things like reading or watching movies.

pitfalls.note: The present of an action verb ending in a vowel takes “-ㄴ다거나”, not “-는다거나”.
pitfalls.en: I do things like watching a movie or reading a book.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㄹ drops it before “-ㄴ다거나”.
pitfalls.en: I do things like hanging out with friends or watching movies.

topik_tip: Pick the form from the stem: vowel gives “-ㄴ다거나”, consonant gives “-는다거나”, ㄹ drops (“논다거나”); adjectives are “-다거나”.

label: doing X, with a side result (reason)
meaning_en: A connective ending for a reason or cause that is an action someone is doing or a state someone claims: “because they were doing X, (an unwelcome or surprising) Y”. It often has the feel of “in the course of trying to X” or “on the pretext of X”.
usage: Verbs take “-ㄴ다고/-는다고” (“잡다 → 잡는다고”, “하다 → 한다고”, “빼다 → 뺀다고”, “만들다 → 만든다고”), adjectives “-다고” (“바쁘다고”), nouns “-(이)라고”. The subjects of the two clauses can differ. The main clause is often something undesirable or unexpected. In everyday speech the collocation “-ㄴ다고 난리다” (making a fuss about doing X) is common. It differs from the quoting “-는다고3”.

examples.en: I sprayed insecticide in an attempt to catch the cockroach.

examples.ko: 민준이가 책을 읽는다고 밤새 불을 켜 놓았어요.
examples.en: Minjun kept the light on all night on account of reading a book.

examples.ko: 동생이 요리를 한다고 부엌을 엉망으로 만들었다.
examples.en: My younger sibling made a mess of the kitchen trying to cook.
Jisu does not even get in touch, claiming to be busy.
These days everyone is making a fuss about losing weight.

compare.difference: “-느라고” takes verbs only and needs the same subject in both clauses. “-는다고” also allows adjectives and a different subject, and often hints that the effort did not pay off.

pair.en: My younger sibling made the kitchen messy trying to cook.
My younger sibling made the kitchen messy because of cooking.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-다고”, never “-ㄴ다고”.
pitfalls.en: Minjun does not even get in touch, claiming to be busy.

topik_tip: Do not translate it as a plain “because”: it describes someone doing or claiming something, and the result is usually a pity or a surprise.

label: but, although (formal)
meaning_en: A formal, mostly written connective ending meaning “but, although”: the second clause contrasts with the first. In the repeated pattern “-으나 -으나” it means “whether ... or ...”.
usage: After a stem ending in a vowel or ㄹ it is “-나”, after other consonants “-으나”. Real stems: “가다 → 가나”, “작다 → 작으나”, “살다 → 사나” (the ㄹ drops), “어렵다 → 어려우나” (ㅂ-irregular), “덥다 → 더우나”, “노력했다 → 노력했으나”; with “이다” it is “이나”. It belongs to news, essays and formal speeches; everyday speech uses “-지만”. The pattern “비가 오나 눈이 오나” means “rain or snow, regardless”.

examples.ko: 민준이는 열심히 노력했으나 결과는 좋지 않았다.
examples.en: Minjun worked hard, but the result was not good.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 어려우나 풀 수 없는 것은 아니다.
examples.en: This problem is difficult, but it is not unsolvable.
The price is high, but the quality is reliable.
On the outside it looks calm, but inside it is uneasy.

examples.ko: 비가 오나 눈이 오나 민준이는 매일 아침 달린다.
examples.en: Rain or snow, Minjun runs every morning.

compare.difference: “-지만” is the everyday form and also fine in writing; “-으나” is formal and mostly written. The meaning is the same.

pair.en: I worked hard, but I failed.
I worked hard, but I failed.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㄹ drops the ㄹ before “-나”.
pitfalls.en: They live in poverty, but their hearts are rich.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우” before the vowel.
pitfalls.wrong: 이 문제는 어렵으나 풀 수 있다.
pitfalls.right: 이 문제는 어려우나 풀 수 있다.
pitfalls.en: This problem is hard, but it can be solved.

topik_tip: “-으나” and “-지만” share a meaning; the register is what tells them apart.

label: because I was busy doing (same subject)
meaning_en: A connective ending for a cause that is the speaker's (or subject's) own activity: “because I was busy doing X, Y (usually a bad result)”. The first action takes up time and energy and that is why the second could not happen.
usage: It attaches to verb stems only, never after “-었-” or “-겠-”. The subject of both clauses must be the same, and the main clause is a statement or question, not a command or suggestion (“공부하느라고 가지 마세요” is wrong). Real stems: “하다 → 하느라고”, “놀다 → 노느라고” (the ㄹ drops), “만들다 → 만드느라고”, “걷다 → 걷느라고”. The main clause is typically negative or about hardship: “못 했다, 늦었다, 바쁘다, 고생하다, 정신이 없다”. A short form “-느라” exists.

examples.en: I could not sleep last night because I was doing homework.
I was in a frenzy looking after the child.

examples.ko: 시험 준비를 하느라고 친구도 못 만났어.
examples.en: I was so busy preparing for the exam that I could not even meet friends.

examples.ko: 영화를 보느라고 전화 온 줄도 몰랐어요.
examples.en: I was watching a movie, so I did not even know a call had come.
I had a hard time writing the report all night.

compare.difference: “-느라고” describes an activity the subject chose to do; “-는 바람에” fits an event that was not planned. Both can be used with a verb, and the translation can look the same.

pair.en: I missed the bus because I was talking with a friend.
I missed the bus because I got to talking with a friend.

compare.difference: “-어서” works for any cause and any subject. “-느라고” is limited to one's own busy activity.

pair.en: I could not sleep because I was doing homework.
I could not sleep because I had a lot of homework.

pitfalls.note: It cannot take a tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I could not sleep because I was doing homework.

pitfalls.note: Both clauses need the same subject; with a different subject use “-는 바람에”.
pitfalls.wrong: 민준이가 노래하느라고 내가 잠을 못 잤다.
pitfalls.right: 민준이가 노래하는 바람에 내가 잠을 못 잤다.
pitfalls.en: Minjun sang, and so I could not sleep.

topik_tip: Same subject, verb stem, no tense ending, negative result: that checklist covers most “-느라고” questions.

label: so that, until, to the point that
meaning_en: A connective ending with three overlapping uses: a purpose (“so that, in order that”), a limit (“until, to the point that”) and a degree. In “-도록 하다” it means “make sure to, see to it that”.
usage: It attaches directly to verb or adjective stems and does not take a tense ending: “크게 말하도록”. The ㄹ stays before ㄷ: “살다 → 살도록”, “만들다 → 만들도록”. As a purpose it is formal and close to “-게”: “들을 수 있도록”, “늦지 않도록”. As a limit it points to the extent: “목이 쉬도록” (until hoarse), “밤새도록” (all night long), “해가 지도록”. Also: “되도록 빨리” (as soon as possible).

examples.ko: 모두가 들을 수 있도록 크게 말해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak loudly so that everyone can hear.
Minjun sang until hoarse.
It snowed all through the night.

examples.ko: 약속 시간에 늦지 않도록 일찍 출발했다.
examples.en: I set off early so that I would not be late for the appointment.

examples.ko: 회의 시간에는 휴대전화를 꺼 두도록 하세요.
examples.en: Please make sure to turn off your phones during the meeting.

compare.difference: In the purpose use “-도록” and “-게” are near-synonyms; “-도록” is a little more formal. Only “-도록” has the “until / to the point that” use.

pair.en: I spoke loudly so that it could be heard well.
I spoke loudly so that it could be heard well.

compare.difference: “-도록 하다” and “-게 하다” overlap when someone is made to do something. “-도록 하세요” is the polite “please make sure to ...”.

pair.en: Please make sure the child goes to bed early.
Please have the child go to bed early.

pitfalls.note: The “until” use does not take a past tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I sang until my voice went hoarse.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-도록”.
pitfalls.wrong: 누구나 쉽게 만드도록 레시피를 단순하게 했다.
pitfalls.right: 누구나 쉽게 만들도록 레시피를 단순하게 했다.
pitfalls.en: I kept the recipe simple so that anyone could make it easily.

topik_tip: In 읽기 answers, “-도록” is “so that” when a goal follows and “until/to the point that” when a result or extreme follows; the two choices are usually clear from the main clause.

label: doing X and taking it along (then Y)
meaning_en: A connective ending for “do X to an object and carry it somewhere, then do Y with it”: the object of the first action is brought to another place. “빵을 사다가 먹다” is “buy bread and bring it to eat it (elsewhere)”.
usage: It attaches to transitive verb stems with the usual “-아/어” vowel (“사다가”, “가져다가”, “빌려다가”, “데려다가”), and the verb after it takes the same object and often a destination. Stems ending in ㅡ drop it (“담그다 → 담가다가”). It contracts to “-어다”: “사다 주다”, “데려다 주다”. Typical: “사다가 주다, 가져다가 놓다, 빌려다가 읽다”. The ending “-다가” alone (interruption) is a different pattern.

examples.ko: 마트에서 우유를 사다가 냉장고에 넣어 두었다.
examples.en: I picked up milk at the supermarket and put it in the fridge.

examples.ko: 친구가 우리 집에 선물을 가져다가 놓고 갔다.
examples.en: My friend brought a present to our house, left it there and went off.

examples.ko: 승규는 나를 집 앞까지 데려다 줬다.
examples.en: Seunggyu took me as far as my doorstep.
I got some kimchi from the neighbors and brought it home to eat.
I picked up the tissue on the floor and threw it in the trash can.
I packed up some side dishes and took them over to share with the neighbors.

compare.difference: “-어서” only says one action follows the other. “-어다가” adds that the object is carried to another place.

pair.en: I bought bread and brought it over to eat.
I bought bread and ate it.

compare.difference: “사다가 주다” and “사 가지고 와서 주다” are near-synonyms. “-어 가지고” is the more spoken form.

pair.en: I bought bread and brought it to give.
I bought bread, came with it and gave it.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㅡ drops it before the vowel: “담그다” becomes “담가”.
pitfalls.en: I made kimchi and took it over to share.

topik_tip: Moving the object is the key: “-어다가” needs an object that travels, as in “사다가, 가져다가, 데려다가”.

label: even if, even though
meaning_en: A concessive connective ending: “even if X, ... / no matter how X, ...”. The first clause does not stop the second from being true, and X may be hypothetical or a fact.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems with the “-아/어” vowel: “오다 → 와도”, “먹다 → 먹어도”, “하다 → 해도”, “쓰다 → 써도”, “듣다 → 들어도” (ㄷ becomes ㄹ), “어렵다 → 어려워도”, “빠르다 → 빨라도”; “학생이다 → 학생이어도”. Often with “아무리” (however much), “-어도 -어도” (no matter how much), and negative or contrasting main clauses. It is not the permission pattern “-어도 되다”.

examples.en: Even if it rains, we will set off as planned.

examples.ko: 아무리 바빠도 밥은 챙겨 먹어야 해요.
examples.en: However busy you are, you have to make sure to eat.

examples.ko: 어려워도 포기하지 말고 끝까지 해 보자.
examples.en: Even if it is hard, let's not give up and try to the end.

examples.ko: 열 번을 들어도 무슨 뜻인지 모르겠어요.
examples.en: Even after hearing it ten times, I do not understand what it means.
No matter how much I eat, I am still hungry.

compare.difference: “-어도” grants a hypothetical or general case (“even if”); “-지만” states a factual contrast (“but”).

pair.en: I will go even if it rains.
It is raining, but I am going.

compare.difference: “-더라도” is a near-synonym that stresses a hypothetical assumption and is a little more formal. Most sentences with “-어도” can use it.

pair.en: It is fine even if you fail.
It is fine even if you fail.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular stem changes ㄷ to ㄹ before a vowel.
pitfalls.en: No matter how much I listen, I do not understand.

pitfalls.note: After a noun the copula is “이어도” (“여도” after a vowel), not “이도”.
pitfalls.en: Even a student has to keep good manners.

topik_tip: Do not mix it up with the permission pattern “-어도 되다”; when no “되다” follows, “-어도” is “even if”.

label: only if, must (necessary condition)
meaning_en: A connective ending that makes the first clause an essential condition: “only if X can Y”, “Y is possible only when X”. In “-어야 소용없다/-어 봐야” it also means “even if, however much”.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems with the “-아/어” vowel: “공부하다 → 공부해야”, “오다 → 와야”, “듣다 → 들어야”, “쉽다 → 쉬워야”, “싸다 → 싸야”; “학생이다 → 학생이어야”. The main clause is usually a present or future judgment (“-ㄹ 수 있다, 되다, 하다”). The emphatic form “-어야만” is a near-synonym. “후회해야 소용없다” means “regretting is useless”.

examples.ko: 열심히 공부해야 시험에 합격할 수 있어요.
examples.en: Only if you study hard can you pass the exam.

examples.ko: 직접 먹어 봐야 맛을 알 수 있다.
examples.en: You can only know the taste by trying it yourself.

examples.ko: 날씨가 좋아야 소풍을 갈 수 있어요.
examples.en: We can go on a picnic only if the weather is good.
Regretting at this point is no use.
Only if the cost is low will many people use it.

compare.difference: “-으면” says X is enough for Y; “-어야” says X is required for Y.

pair.en: If you study, you pass.
Only if you study do you pass.

compare.difference: “-어야만” is the same pattern with “만” added for emphasis; the meaning is the same and the tone firmer.

pair.en: It improves only with practice.
It improves only with practice.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우” and adds “-어”: “쉽다” becomes “쉬워”.
pitfalls.en: Only if the problem is easy can they solve it.

topik_tip: Contrast “-으면” (sufficient) and “-어야” (necessary): the second says “only if”.

label: only if (emphatic condition)
meaning_en: A connective ending that makes the first clause an essential condition for the second: “only if you X, Y”. It is the emphatic, spoken partner of “-어야”, and the main clause often ends in “-지”.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems with the “-아/어” vowel: “노력하다 → 노력해야지”, “쉽다 → 쉬워야지” (ㅂ-irregular), “깨끗하다 → 깨끗해야지”, “학생이다 → 학생이어야지”. The main clause states a possibility or result and typically ends in “-지(요)”, which adds the speaker's firm tone: “노력해야지 성공하지”. The same ending also closes sentences (“이제 공부해야지”) as a self-reminder or resolution; that is a separate use of the form.

examples.ko: 책을 많이 읽어야지 글을 잘 쓰지.
examples.en: You write well only if you read a lot.
You will not be late only if you get up early.
You get energy only if you eat.
Fish can live only when the water is clear.
From now on, I should read books.

compare.difference: “-어야” and “-어야지” both make the first clause a necessary condition. “-어야지” is more spoken and more insistent, usually with “-지” in the main clause.

pair.en: You pass only if you study.
You pass only if you study, you know.

compare.difference: At the end of a sentence “-어야지” is the speaker's resolution or reminder (“I should ...”), not a condition.

pair.en: Now I should study.
You pass only if you study, you know.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우” before the vowel: “쉽다” becomes “쉬워”.
pitfalls.en: They can solve the problem only if it is easy.

topik_tip: The connective reading needs a second clause; when “-어야지” ends the sentence, the meaning shifts to “I should/will”.

label: when I did X, (I found) Y
meaning_en: A connective ending for a result the speaker observed after their own action or state: “when/after I did X, Y happened”. The first clause is the speaker's own past action, and the second is what followed, seen first-hand.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems: “먹다 → 먹었더니”, “가다 → 갔더니”, “하다 → 했더니”, “듣다 → 들었더니”, “눕다 → 누웠더니” (ㅂ-irregular). The agent of the first clause is normally the speaker (“I”, or “we”), and the second clause reports what happened, in the past or as a present state (“열이 내렸다, 피곤하다”). The result is something observed, so it does not become a command or a future plan. Typical frame: “갔더니 ...(이)/가 있었다/없었다”.

examples.en: After I took the medicine, my fever went down.
When I went home, nobody was there.

examples.ko: 어제 밤늦게까지 책을 읽었더니 오늘 너무 피곤해요.
examples.en: I read until late last night, so I am very tired today.

examples.ko: 민준이에게 말을 걸었더니 민준이가 활짝 웃었다.
examples.en: When I spoke to Minjun, Minjun smiled broadly.
I lay down in bed and fell asleep right away.

compare.difference: “-었더니” is for what happened after the speaker's own action. “-더니” reports what the speaker saw of someone else, and then the change that followed.

pair.en: I studied hard, and my grades went up.
Minjun studied hard, and then their grades went up.

compare.difference: For discovery the two are near-synonyms (“문을 열었더니” / “문을 여니까”). “-으니까” can also give a reason for a command; “-었더니” cannot.

pair.en: When I opened the door, wind blew in.
When I opened the door, wind blew in.

pitfalls.note: The result clause is something observed, so it is not a command.
pitfalls.en: When I went home, nobody was there.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular stem becomes “우” plus “-었-”: “눕다” gives “누웠더니”.
pitfalls.en: I lay down in bed and fell asleep.

topik_tip: Look for the speaker as agent in the first clause and an observed result in the second.

label: as soon as
meaning_en: A connective ending meaning “as soon as, the moment X”: the second event follows the first immediately. The subjects of the two clauses may be the same or different.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with no tense ending: “하다 → 하자마자”, “눕다 → 눕자마자”, “듣다 → 듣자마자”; the ㄹ of a ㄹ-stem stays (“놀다 → 놀자마자”, “만들다 → 만들자마자”). The tense is on the main verb. It needs an action verb, so a plain state such as “따뜻하다” takes “-아/어지다” first (“따뜻해지자마자”). Frequent collocations: “눈을 뜨자마자” (the moment I open my eyes), “도착하자마자”, “집에 오자마자”.

examples.en: I took a shower as soon as I got home.
I fell asleep the moment I lay down.
Minjun left the classroom as soon as class ended.
Jisu heard the news and ran to the hospital right away.
The moment I open my eyes, I check my phone first.

compare.difference: “-자마자” stresses that there is no gap; “-고 나서” only says that the second event comes after the first is finished.

pair.en: I went out the moment I had washed.
I washed and then went out.

compare.difference: “-는 대로” (as soon as) is a near-synonym that is often heard with requests and plans (“도착하는 대로 전화해 주세요”). “-자마자” is the usual choice for narrating what happened right after something.

pair.en: I called as soon as I arrived.
I will call as soon as I arrive.

pitfalls.note: It takes no tense ending; the tense goes on the final verb.
pitfalls.en: I called as soon as I arrived.

pitfalls.note: A plain state does not take it; a change of state does.
pitfalls.en: As soon as the weather turned warm, the flowers bloomed.

topik_tip: “-자마자” never takes “-었-”: “도착하자마자”, not “도착했자마자”.

label: while doing X, Y happened; because of X
meaning_en: A connective ending with three uses besides plain interruption: something happens while an action is in progress (“while doing X, Y came up”), the first action causes the second (“doing too much X, so Y”), and two things alternate (“-다가 -다가”).
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems (“보다 → 보다가”, “듣다 → 듣다가”, “걷다 → 걷다가”, “살다 → 살다가”, “춥다 → 춥다가”); the ㄷ of “걷다” does not change before “-다가”. The main clause is usually a past event that breaks into the activity: “영화를 보다가 ...을 떠올렸다”. For the cause use the main clause often says something bad: “과식을 하다가 배탈이 났다”. The repeated shape “울다가 웃다가 하다” is about alternation. Compare the level-2 lesson, which covers switching from one action to another.

examples.ko: 영화를 보다가 갑자기 그 사람이 생각났다.
examples.en: While watching a movie, I suddenly thought of that person.
While walking down the street, I ran into an old friend.
I overate and got an upset stomach.
I got sleepy while driving, so I rested for a bit.

examples.ko: 아이가 울다가 웃다가 하면서 금방 기분이 바뀐다.
examples.en: The child's mood changes quickly, crying, then laughing, then crying again.

compare.difference: “-는 동안” covers the whole stretch of time. “-다가” picks a moment inside the activity, and that activity is cut into.

pair.en: Do not doze off while you are driving.
I dozed off while driving.

compare.difference: “-다 보니” reports what one realised after carrying on with an activity for a while. “-다가” is an event that breaks in.

pair.en: I dozed off while reading.
As I kept reading, it had become dawn before I knew it.

pitfalls.note: The ㄷ of “걷다” stays before “-다가”; it becomes ㄹ only before a vowel.
pitfalls.en: While walking down the street, I ran into a friend.

topik_tip: Both “-다가1(1)” and “-다가1(2)” are the same ending in the list; this row stands for “while doing X, Y occurred / because of X”.

label: since, as (reason or premise)
meaning_en: A connective ending that gives the reason, cause or premise for the main clause: “since X, Y”. Because it sets a premise, the main clause can be a command, suggestion or judgment. It also introduces what one finds after doing something: “열어 보니 ...”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-니”, after other consonants “-으니”. Real stems: “있다 → 있으니”, “살다 → 사니” (the ㄹ drops), “만들다 → 만드니”, “춥다 → 추우니” (ㅂ-irregular), “듣다 → 들으니” (ㄷ-irregular), “낫다 → 나으니”, “이다 → (이)니”; with “-었-”: “끝났으니”. It is shorter and more written than “-으니까” but takes the same kinds of main clauses, including “-세요, -자, -ㄹ까”.

examples.ko: 날씨가 이렇게 추우니 옷을 따뜻하게 입고 가세요.
examples.en: It is this cold, so wear warm clothes when you go.
I have been standing for a long time, so my legs hurt.
Class is over now, so you may go home.

examples.ko: 식구가 많으니 집 안이 늘 북적거린다.
examples.en: There are many people in the family, so the house is always bustling.

examples.ko: 길이 이렇게 막히니 약속 시간에 늦을 수밖에 없다.
examples.en: With traffic this heavy, being late for the appointment is unavoidable.

compare.difference: “-으니까” is the everyday form and can close a sentence (“-으니까요”); “-으니” is shorter and more written. With a command both work.

pair.en: It is cold, so wear a coat when you go.
It is cold, so wear a coat when you go.

compare.difference: “-어서” cannot be followed by a command or a suggestion. “-으니” can.

pair.en: It is cold, so wear a coat when you go.
It was cold, so I put on a coat.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우”.
pitfalls.en: It is cold, so dress warmly.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㄹ drops it before “-니”.
pitfalls.wrong: 이 도시에 오래 살으니 정이 들었다.
pitfalls.right: 이 도시에 오래 사니 정이 들었다.
pitfalls.en: Having lived in this city a long time, I have grown fond of it.

topik_tip: “-으니” can introduce a reason or a discovery; “-어서” is the one that refuses a command in the main clause.

label: if you want to, in order to
meaning_en: A connective ending for the condition of having an intention: “if you want to X, then (you need) Y”. The main clause names what is needed or advisable. It is a contraction of “-으려고 하면”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-려면”, after other consonants “-으려면”; it attaches to verb stems only. The ㄹ of a ㄹ-stem stays: “살다 → 살려면”, “만들다 → 만들려면”. Irregular verbs: “걷다 → 걸으려면” (ㄷ becomes ㄹ), “눕다 → 누우려면”, “낫다 → 나으려면”. The main clause is a requirement or advice (“-어야 하다, -는 게 좋다, -ㄹ 수 없다”), rarely a past event.

examples.en: To be good at Korean, you have to practise every day.

examples.ko: 서울역에 가려면 어느 쪽으로 가야 해요?
examples.en: Which way do I have to go to get to Seoul Station?

examples.ko: 건강하게 오래 살려면 규칙적으로 운동하는 게 좋다.
examples.en: To live long and healthy, it is good to exercise regularly.

examples.ko: 이 일을 끝내려면 밤을 새울 수밖에 없다.
examples.en: To finish this job, there is no choice but to stay up all night.
To buy a ticket, you need an ID.

compare.difference: “-으려고” states the goal of an action that is done (“I study in order to pass”). “-으려면” sets the goal as a condition for what is needed.

pair.en: I study in order to pass.
To pass, you have to study.

compare.difference: “-기 위해(서)” and “-으려면” are close when the main clause says what is needed. “-으려면” makes the goal a condition.

pair.en: In order to pass, one has to study.
To pass, you have to study.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ: “사려면” would be “to buy” from “사다”.
pitfalls.en: To live long, you have to be healthy.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular verb turns ㄷ into ㄹ before “-으”.
pitfalls.en: To walk fast, you need sneakers.

topik_tip: Do not mix the ㄹ-stem “살려면” (to live) with “사려면” (to buy).

label: recalled, unfinished or habitual past modifier
meaning_en: An adnominal ending that modifies a noun with a past action that was habitual, ongoing or left unfinished (“the house I used to live in”, “the book I was reading”), or a past state (“the winter that was cold”).
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and to “이다”: “살다 → 살던”, “읽다 → 읽던”, “춥다 → 춥던” (ㅂ stays, since “-던” begins with a consonant), “만들다 → 만들던” (ㄹ stays), “학생이던”. With a verb it means “used to do” or “was doing, and did not finish”; for a completed event the ending is “-었던” or “-은”. Typical: “자주 가던 식당”, “쓰던 연필”, “살던 곳”. It cannot take “다” (all) or a clearly finished result.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 살던 집에 다시 가 보았다.
examples.en: I went to see again the house where I lived as a child.

examples.ko: 읽던 책을 책상 위에 두고 나갔다.
examples.en: I left the book I was reading on the desk and went out.

examples.ko: 우리가 자주 가던 식당이 문을 닫았다.
examples.en: The restaurant we used to go to often has closed.

examples.ko: 이 노래는 어머니가 자주 부르시던 노래예요.
examples.en: This song is one my mother often sang.

examples.ko: 늘 웃던 지수가 오늘은 표정이 어두웠다.
examples.en: Jisu, who always used to smile, looked gloomy today.

compare.difference: “-은” (verbs) points to a completed event. “-던” points to an action that was in progress or repeated, or was left unfinished.

pair.en: I left the bread I was eating.
The bread I ate was tasty.

compare.difference: “살던 집” and “살았던 집” are near-synonyms for a past home. “-었던” presents the period as over; only “-던” also covers an action that stopped midway.

pair.en: I miss the house I used to live in.
I miss the house I lived in.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective keeps its ㅂ before “-던”: the change to “우” happens only before a vowel.
pitfalls.en: The cold winter passed and spring came.

pitfalls.note: “-던” leaves an action unfinished, so it does not go with “다” (all, completely).
pitfalls.en: I returned the book I had finished reading to the library.

topik_tip: Unfinished or repeated gives “-던”; finished gives “-은/-었던”.

label: explaining the reason (“you see”)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with which the speaker gives a reason or background that the listener may not know yet: “...because, you see”, often followed by more of the story. It is the “해체” form; the polite version is “-거든요”.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems, and also after “-었-/-겠-”: “있다 → 있거든”, “가다 → 가거든”, “생일이다 → 생일이거든”, “받았다 → 받았거든”. The sentence it ends is the reason, placed after the thing it explains (“배고파. 아침을 안 먹었거든.”). It presents new information, not something both people know. To a person you speak politely to, add “요”. It does not form questions or commands.

examples.ko: 저는 먼저 갈게요. 내일 일찍 일어나야 하거든요.
examples.en: I will head out first. I have to get up early tomorrow, you see.

examples.ko: 요즘 한국어를 배우고 있어요. 한국 드라마를 좋아하거든요.
examples.en: I am learning Korean these days. I like Korean dramas, you see.
Today is on me. I got paid, you see.

examples.ko: 내일 내 생일이거든. 부모님이 무슨 선물을 주실까?
examples.en: Tomorrow is my birthday, you see. I wonder what gift my parents will give me.

examples.ko: 지수는 지금 못 와요. 아직 회의 중이거든요.
examples.en: Jisu cannot come now. They are still in a meeting, you see.

compare.difference: “-거든” gives the listener new information as a reason. “-잖아” reminds the listener of something they already know.

pair.en: I am hungry. I did not eat breakfast, you see.
I am hungry. I did not eat breakfast, remember.

compare.difference: “-어서” joins the reason before the result in one sentence. “-거든” puts the reason after the result as its own sentence.

pair.en: I am hungry because I did not eat breakfast.
I am hungry. I did not eat breakfast, you see.

pitfalls.note: With someone you speak politely to, add “요”: the bare “-거든” is the “해체” form.
pitfalls.wrong: 선생님, 저 먼저 갈게요. 약속이 있거든.
pitfalls.right: 선생님, 저 먼저 갈게요. 약속이 있거든요.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, I will be going first. I have an appointment, you see.

pitfalls.note: The sentence with “-거든” is the reason itself, not the result.
pitfalls.en: I am hungry. I did not eat breakfast, you see.

topik_tip: The curriculum tags this row as “이유” (reason); the sentence it ends is the explanation, and it can leave the story open.

label: noticing something new (exclamation)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that voices the speaker's realisation of a fact they have just noticed or learned: “I see, so ...”, “oh, it ...”. It is the “해라체” form of this exclamation, so it is spoken to friends and younger people, or to oneself.
usage: Verbs and “있다/없다” take “-는구나” (“오다 → 오는구나”, “있다 → 있구나/있는구나”, “살다 → 사는구나” with the ㄹ dropped); adjectives and “이다” take “-구나” (“춥다 → 춥구나”, “학생이다 → 학생이구나”); past forms take “-었구나” (“갔구나”). Polite counterparts are “-는군요” or “-네요”. It reports the speaker's own fresh discovery, so it is not used for something one has long known. “아, 그렇구나” is the set phrase meaning “oh, I see”.

examples.en: The night has already grown deep.
You are taller than I thought.
Oh, it is snowing outside.
Oh, so you are Jisu's younger sibling.
Oh, I see. I did not know.

compare.difference: “-네” is a light, spoken exclamation of noticing and also has the polite “-네요”. “-는구나” is the “해라체” form.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing.
Oh, it is snowing.

compare.difference: “-는구나” reacts to something noticed now. “-더라” reports what the speaker saw or experienced earlier.

pair.en: Oh, it is snowing.
I saw that it was snowing.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-구나”, not “-는구나”.
pitfalls.en: It is cold, I see.

pitfalls.note: A past stem takes “-구나”, not “-는구나”.
pitfalls.en: It rained yesterday, I see.

topik_tip: Check the stem: action verb gives “-는구나”, adjective or past stem gives “-구나”.

label: plain present statement (“한다체”)
meaning_en: The plain declarative ending of written Korean: verbs take “-ㄴ다/-는다”, adjectives and “이다” take “-다”. It is the “한다체”, used in news, essays, diaries and fiction narration, and in speech to children or close friends.
usage: Verbs ending in a vowel take “-ㄴ다” (“가다 → 간다”, “하다 → 한다”), verbs ending in a consonant “-는다” (“먹다 → 먹는다”, “읽다 → 읽는다”), ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (“살다 → 산다”, “만들다 → 만든다”). Adjectives and “이다” take bare “-다” (“높다”, “학생이다”); “있다/없다” also take “-다”. The past is “-었다”, the future “-ㄹ 것이다”. It is the style that longer 쓰기 answers expect, not the polite “해요체”.

examples.ko: 나는 매일 아침 일곱 시에 일어난다.
examples.en: I get up at seven every morning.
The children play in the park, kicking a ball.

examples.ko: 정부는 다음 달부터 새로운 제도를 시행한다.
examples.en: The government will put a new system into effect from next month.
Jisu eats bread every morning.
Minjun exercises every day.

compare.difference: “-어” is the spoken “해체” ending; “-는다” is the written “한다체”. The meaning is the same.

pair.en: Minjun goes to school.
Minjun goes to school.

compare.difference: “-습니다” is the formal polite “합쇼체” (speeches, announcements). “-는다” is plain and used where no listener is addressed.

pair.en: I exercise every day.
I exercise every day.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes bare “-다”.
pitfalls.en: The sky is high.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-ㄴ다”.
pitfalls.en: We live in Seoul.

topik_tip: In 쓰기 writing tasks, pick the plain “-ㄴ다/-는다” style and stay with it to the end.

label: I saw that ... (recalled observation)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with which the speaker reports something they saw, heard or experienced in the past, often with a note of surprise or admiration, and leaves room for the listener to react. The polite form is “-던데요”.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems: “하다 → 하던데”, “맛있다 → 맛있던데”, “학생이다 → 학생이던데”; with “-었-” it refers to a finished event (“안 왔던데”). It reports what the speaker has observed first-hand, usually about someone or something else, not the speaker's own plain action. It often introduces a point that contrasts with what the listener thinks, or is followed by a suggestion. It is the “해체” form; add “요” when speaking politely.

examples.ko: 어제 보니까 민준이가 노래를 정말 잘하던데.
examples.en: I saw it yesterday, and Minjun really sings well.

examples.ko: 그 식당 음식이 아주 맛있던데, 한번 가 봐.
examples.en: The food at that restaurant was really good, so give it a try.
Jisu did not come to the office yesterday, I noticed.

examples.ko: 밖에 비가 많이 오던데 우산 가져가.
examples.en: It was raining a lot outside, so take an umbrella.
The roads were especially jammed today.

compare.difference: “-더라” and “-던데” both report an observation. “-더라” just states it; “-던데” sounds more open-ended and often leads into a contrast or suggestion.

pair.en: That movie was fun.
That movie was fun, though.

compare.difference: “-는데” is about what the speaker sees now; “-던데” about what the speaker saw earlier.

pair.en: It is snowing outside.
It was snowing outside.

pitfalls.note: It reports what the speaker observed, not their own plain action.
pitfalls.en: The movie I saw yesterday was really fun.

pitfalls.note: With someone you speak politely to, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, that restaurant was good, you know.

topik_tip: Read it as “I noticed that ...”: it signals the speaker's own recalled observation.

label: reminding, “you know”, “remember”
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending (from “-지 않아”) with which the speaker reminds the listener of something both of them know or should know, often to give a reason, or to correct or complain. The polite form is “-잖아요”.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems and to “-었-”: “오늘은 일요일이잖아”, “맛있잖아”, “어제 말했잖아”. The content is treated as shared knowledge, so it is the opposite of “-거든”, which gives new information. It can have a scolding tone, so with a person you must be polite to, use “-잖아요” carefully. Spelling: “그렇잖아”, not “그렇찮아”. The discourse marker “있잖아” (you know what; listen) opens a new topic.

examples.ko: 오늘은 일요일이잖아. 회사 안 가도 돼.
examples.en: It is Sunday, remember? You do not have to go to work.

examples.ko: 너도 알잖아. 나는 매운 음식을 못 먹어.
examples.en: You know that, don't you? I cannot eat spicy food.
I told you yesterday. That I have an appointment today.

examples.ko: 아까 비가 왔잖아. 그래서 길이 아직 젖어 있어.
examples.en: It rained a while ago, remember? So the road is still wet.
You know what, I have something to say.

compare.difference: “-잖아” points to something the listener already knows. “-거든” offers a reason the listener does not know yet.

pair.en: It is Monday, remember.
It is Monday, you see.

compare.difference: “-지” asks for gentle confirmation. “-잖아” says the thing is obvious and often carries a hint of reproach.

pair.en: This one is the tastiest, isn't it?
This one is the tastiest, remember.

pitfalls.note: To a person you owe politeness, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Senior, you have already read this book, remember?

pitfalls.note: The spelling is “잖”: it comes from “지 않아”.
pitfalls.en: You are like that too.

topik_tip: In listening items, “-잖아” signals that the speaker treats the content as already known to the listener.

label: let's (suggestion)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that proposes doing something together: “let's ...”. It is the “해라체” suggestion and belongs to speech between friends, to younger people, and to slogans.
usage: It attaches to verb stems only; the ㄹ of a ㄹ-stem stays (“놀다 → 놀자”, “만들다 → 만들자”). The negative is “-지 말자”. It is not used to a person you owe respect: the polite counterparts are “-어요” and “-ㅂ시다/-으시지요”. Slogans and posters use it too (“에너지를 아끼자”). Common combinations: “같이 -자”, “-어 보자”, “-러 가자”.

examples.en: Let's eat together this evening.
Let's go see a movie this weekend.
It is late, so let's go now.
Let's give it a try together.
Let's all save energy.

compare.difference: “-자” is a direct proposal. “-을까” makes it a question and leaves the decision open.

pair.en: Let's have lunch.
Shall we have lunch?

compare.difference: “-자” is for equals and juniors. “-어요” can also suggest, in the polite “해요체”.

pair.en: Let's go together.
Let's go together.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-자”.
pitfalls.en: Let's make a cake together.

pitfalls.note: The negative suggestion is “-지 말자”.
pitfalls.en: Let's not fight.

topik_tip: The “-자” suggestion is limited to verbs; for adjectives and a polite tone, other endings are used.

label: asking a friendly question
meaning_en: A sentence-final question ending: “-니?” asks a question in the “해라체”. The tone is gentle and caring, as in an adult speaking to a child, a sibling, or a friend.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems and to “-었-/-겠-”: “가다 → 가니”, “먹다 → 먹었니”, “예쁘다 → 예쁘니”, “학생이다 → 학생이니”. A stem ending in ㄹ drops it before “니”: “살다 → 사니”, “놀다 → 노니”, “만들다 → 만드니”. A ㅂ-irregular stem keeps ㅂ, as “니” starts with a consonant: “춥다 → 춥니”. It is used to people you can speak down to; with a person you owe politeness it is “-어요” or “-ㅂ니까”. The dictionary also lists a rare statement use of “-니”; the question is the form in everyday speech.

examples.en: Did you eat breakfast properly?
How have you been lately?

examples.ko: 어디 아프니? 얼굴이 안 좋아 보여.
examples.en: Are you sick? You do not look well.
Is this book fun?
Where do you live?

compare.difference: “-니?” is the “해라체” question and sounds gentle. “-어?” is the casual “해체” question that fits people on equal terms.

pair.en: What are you doing?
What are you doing?

compare.difference: “-습니까” is the formal polite question of the “합쇼체”; “-니” is for those you speak down to.

pair.en: Where are you going?
Where are you going?

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “니”.
pitfalls.en: Where do you live?

pitfalls.note: It is not for someone you owe politeness.
pitfalls.en: Grandmother, have you eaten?

topik_tip: It is a question ending only; the statement “-니” of the dictionary entry is a different, rare use.

label: make or let someone do
meaning_en: A causative expression: “make someone do, let someone do, have someone do”, and with an adjective “make it ...”: “행복하게 하다” (make happy). The subject causes or allows another person or thing to act.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems: “먹다 → 먹게 하다”, “가다 → 가게 하다”, “행복하다 → 행복하게 하다”. The one who acts takes “을/를” or “에게” (“아이를 가게 했다”, “아이에게 가게 했다”); if that verb has an object of its own, the actor takes “에게/한테” so that “을” is not doubled (“아이에게 채소를 먹게 했다”). It covers both “force” and “permit”, depending on context.

examples.en: Mom made the child eat vegetables.

examples.ko: 선생님이 학생들을 일찍 집에 가게 하셨다.
examples.en: The teacher let the students go home early.
This music makes me happy.
My parents let my younger sibling go study abroad.
That movie made the audience cry.

compare.difference: “-게 만들다” stresses causing a result, and cannot mean “let”. “-게 하다” also covers permission.

pair.en: I had the child go to bed early.
I made the child go to bed early.

compare.difference: A lexical causative like “먹이다” means to feed; “-게 하다” has the other person eat.

pair.en: Mom fed the child.
Mom had the child eat.

pitfalls.note: A second “를” in the same clause is avoided: the one who acts takes “에게”.
pitfalls.en: Mom made the child eat vegetables.

topik_tip: The list also notes “-게 만들다” and “-도록 하다” as related expressions.

label: after finishing X
meaning_en: An expression for “after having finished X”: the first action is complete, and what follows depends on that. Mostly seen as “-고 나서”, “-고 나니(까)” (after doing, I found ...) and “-고 나면” (once X is done).
usage: It attaches to verb stems; “나다” itself takes the endings: “-고 나서” (then), “-고 나니” (and then I found), “-고 나면” (once ... is done), “-고 나자” (right after). The first verb has no tense ending (“먹었고 나서” is wrong). The “나서” form is the plain sequence marker and the others add the speaker's finding or a condition. Frequent collocation: “울고 나니”, “먹고 나서”, “하고 나면”.

examples.en: Please take the medicine after you eat.
After I finished my homework, I felt lighter.
Once I have exercised, I feel better.

examples.ko: 영화를 보고 나서 친구와 이야기를 나눴다.
examples.en: After watching the movie, I talked with my friend.
After a good cry, I feel relieved.

compare.difference: “-고 나서” and “-은 후에” are near-synonyms for “after”. “-고 나서” puts the stress on the first action being done.

pair.en: After I finished eating, I took the medicine.
After I ate, I took the medicine.

compare.difference: “-고” simply links actions in order; “-고 나서” adds that the first is completed before the second.

pair.en: I ate and went to school.
After I finished eating, I went to school.

pitfalls.note: The first verb takes no past ending.
pitfalls.en: After I finished eating, I took the medicine.

topik_tip: Tell the forms apart: “-고 나서” (then), “-고 나니” (and I found), “-고 나면” (once X is done).

label: end up doing, or resolve to
meaning_en: An expression for an outcome that happened in the end, often against the speaker's wish: “end up doing, go and do”. With “-겠-” or “-ㄹ 것이다” it is resolve: “I will do it, no matter what”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: “넘어지다 → 넘어지고 말았다”. The past “-고 말았다” expresses regret, finality or an unintended result (often with “결국, 그만, 끝내”). “-고 말겠다/-고 말 것이다” shows determination (“합격하고 말겠다”). It is not used with adjectives. It is close to “-어 버리다”, but “-고 말다” stresses that the event could not be avoided.

examples.en: I was running in a rush and ended up falling over.

examples.ko: 아껴 둔 과자를 동생이 먹고 말았다.
examples.en: My younger sibling went and ate the snacks I had saved.

examples.ko: 참으려고 했지만 결국 눈물을 터뜨리고 말았다.
examples.en: I tried to hold back, but in the end I burst into tears.
I will pass this time, no matter what.
Minjun ended up forgetting an important appointment.

compare.difference: Both can mean something is done and over. “-어 버리다” can be relief or neutral; “-고 말다” leans toward regret or resolve.

pair.en: I ended up losing my phone.
I lost my phone.

pitfalls.note: It attaches to verbs, not adjectives.
pitfalls.en: In the end, it rained.

topik_tip: “-고 말았다” is regret or unavoidability; “-고 말겠다” is determination. The tense and the subject's attitude tell which.

label: wants to (someone else)
meaning_en: An expression for what a third person wants to do: “wants to, would like to”. It is the “-고 싶다” of the speaker turned into something observed about someone else: verb stem + “-고 싶어 하다”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems: “가다 → 가고 싶어 하다”, “되다 → 되고 싶어 하다”. “-고 싶다” expresses the speaker's own wish (or the listener's, in a question). For a third person in plain statements, “싶어 하다” is normally used: the desire is described from outside. The object takes “을/를”, not “이/가” (“물을 마시고 싶어 한다”). In the modifier form it is “-고 싶어 하는” (“민준이가 먹고 싶어 하는 음식”). The “하다” is conjugated: “싶어 한다, 싶어 했다, 싶어 해요”.

examples.ko: 해외여행을 가고 싶어 하는 동생에게 여행 책을 사 주었다.
examples.en: I bought a travel book for my younger sibling, who wants to travel abroad.

examples.ko: 놀이공원에 가고 싶어 하는 아이들이 줄을 서 있다.
examples.en: Children who want to go to the amusement park are lined up.

examples.ko: 지수는 한국어 선생님이 되고 싶어 해요.
examples.en: Jisu wants to become a Korean teacher.

examples.ko: 우리 강아지는 산책하러 나가고 싶어 한다.
examples.en: Our dog wants to go out for a walk.

examples.ko: 민준이가 먹고 싶어 하는 음식을 시켰어요.
examples.en: I ordered the food that Minjun wants to eat.

compare.difference: “-고 싶다” is the speaker's own wish. “-고 싶어 하다” describes someone else's wish.

pair.en: I want to rest.
Minjun wants to rest.

compare.difference: “-고 싶어 하다” reports the wish as seen. “-고 싶은가 보다” is the speaker's guess about it.

pair.en: Minjun wants to rest.
Minjun seems to want to rest.

pitfalls.note: In a plain statement about a third person, “-고 싶다” is normally not used.
pitfalls.en: Minjun wants to travel.

pitfalls.note: The object of “싶어 하다” takes “을/를”.
pitfalls.en: Minjun wants to drink water.

topik_tip: Third person with “싶어 하다”, first person with “싶다”: the choice is a standard grammar item.

label: as a result of doing X
meaning_en: A written expression meaning “as a result of doing X”: it introduces what a process of investigation, discussion or analysis turned up.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with the past modifier “-ㄴ/-은”: “조사하다 → 조사한 결과”, “분석하다 → 분석한 결과”, “토론하다 → 토론한 결과”, “만들다 → 만든 결과” (the ㄹ drops). The main clause states the finding or the decision that followed: “-것으로 나타났다, -것으로 밝혀졌다, -기로 했다”. It belongs to news, reports and academic prose. The noun “결과” stays spaced: “조사 결과” is also common without the verb.

examples.ko: 설문 조사를 한 결과 응답자의 70퍼센트가 찬성했다.
examples.en: As a result of the survey, 70 percent of the respondents were in favor.

examples.ko: 여러 번 실험한 결과 같은 값이 나왔다.
examples.en: As a result of experimenting many times, the same value came out.

examples.ko: 의사와 상담한 결과 수술을 하기로 결정했다.
examples.en: After consulting the doctor, we decided to have the operation.

examples.ko: 오랜 시간 토론한 결과 계획을 바꾸기로 했다.
examples.en: After discussing it for a long time, we decided to change the plan.

examples.ko: 원인을 분석한 결과 소프트웨어 오류로 밝혀졌다.
examples.en: Analysis of the cause revealed a software error.

compare.difference: “-은 후에” only says what came later. “-은 결과” says the second clause is the outcome of the first.

pair.en: As a result of the investigation, a problem was found.
After the investigation, I wrote a report.

compare.difference: “-은 끝에” stresses a long effort or process before the result. “-은 결과” reports the findings of a process in a neutral way.

pair.en: As a result of long thought, I decided to change jobs.
After long deliberation, I decided to change jobs.

pitfalls.note: It takes the past modifier of a verb.
pitfalls.en: As a result of the investigation, a problem was found.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-ㄴ”.
pitfalls.wrong: 여러 번 만들은 결과 맛이 좋아졌다.
pitfalls.right: 여러 번 만든 결과 맛이 좋아졌다.
pitfalls.en: After making it many times, the taste improved.

topik_tip: News and report passages use “-은 결과” to introduce a finding; the finding comes in the main clause.

label: after X is done
meaning_en: An expression meaning “after X is done”: it puts the second action in the step following the first. It is natural in instructions, plans and step-by-step explanations.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with the past modifier “-ㄴ/-은”: “씻다 → 씻은 다음에”, “끓다 → 끓은 다음에”, “끝나다 → 끝난 다음에”, “만들다 → 만든 다음에” (the ㄹ drops). “다음에” is written with a space. The meaning is the same as “-은 후에” and “-은 뒤에”. The main clause may be a command, a plan or a past event. Common: “졸업한 다음에”, “끝난 다음에”, and “그 다음에” (and then).

examples.en: Eat after you wash your hands.
Put in the ramen after the water boils.

examples.ko: 숙제를 다 한 다음에 놀러 나갈게요.
examples.en: I will go out to play after I finish all my homework.

examples.ko: 졸업한 다음에 무엇을 할지 아직 정하지 못했다.
examples.en: I have not yet decided what to do after graduating.
Let's talk after the meeting is over.

compare.difference: “-은 다음에” and “-은 후에” are near-synonyms. “다음에” fits step-by-step order.

pair.en: Take the medicine after you eat.
Take the medicine after you eat.

compare.difference: “-기 전에” is the opposite: it names the later step first (“before”), with the verb in the base form.

pair.en: Eat after you wash.
Wash before you eat.

pitfalls.note: The modifier is past; a present modifier does not fit “after”.
pitfalls.en: Take the medicine after you eat.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-ㄴ”.
pitfalls.en: After making the cake, I packaged it.

topik_tip: “-은 다음에” and “-은 후에/뒤에” are interchangeable in nearly all test sentences.

label: instead of; in return
meaning_en: An expression with two linked meanings: “instead of doing X” (a replacement) and “X is so, but in return/on the other hand Y” (a trade-off between a disadvantage and a compensation).
usage: Verbs take “-는 대신(에)” (“먹다 → 먹는 대신에”, “만들다 → 만드는 대신에”, the ㄹ drops); adjectives take “-ㄴ/은 대신(에)” (“비싸다 → 비싼 대신에”, “춥다 → 추운 대신에”); a noun takes “N 대신(에)” (“커피 대신에 차”). The “에” is optional. In the trade-off use the two clauses balance each other: a minus in one, a plus in the other (or an exchange of favours: “내가 하는 대신에 네가 해”). Spacing: “대신에” is a separate word.

examples.ko: 오늘은 밥을 먹는 대신에 샐러드를 먹었다.
examples.en: Today I ate a salad instead of rice.

examples.ko: 이 집은 값이 비싼 대신에 음식이 아주 맛있다.
examples.en: This place is expensive, but in return the food is very good.

examples.ko: 설거지는 내가 하는 대신에 청소는 네가 해.
examples.en: I will do the dishes, and in exchange you do the cleaning.

examples.ko: 우리 동네는 교통이 불편한 대신에 공기가 맑다.
examples.en: Our neighborhood has inconvenient transport, but the air is clean.
I drank tea instead of coffee.

compare.difference: Both can contrast two sides of one thing. “-는 대신에” adds the idea of compensation or exchange; “-는 반면” simply sets two facts against each other.

pair.en: It is expensive, but in return it is tasty.
It is expensive, whereas it is tasty.

compare.difference: In the “instead of” use, “-는 대신에” and “-지 않고” are close. “-지 않고” just denies the first action.

pair.en: I ate bread instead of rice.
I did not eat rice and ate bread.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은”, not “-는”.
pitfalls.en: It is expensive, but in return it is tasty.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-는”.
pitfalls.en: Instead of making it at home, I bought it.

topik_tip: Both readings appear in tests: pick “instead of” when the two actions replace each other, and “in return” when a plus balances a minus.

label: to the extent that; in proportion to
meaning_en: A modifier plus the dependent noun “만큼” that means “as much as, to the extent that, in proportion to”. It also gives a reason that fits the main clause: “since it is X, (it is only right that) Y”.
usage: Verbs take “-는 만큼” for the present, “-ㄴ/은 만큼” for the past and “-ㄹ/을 만큼” for an extent or the future (“노력하는 만큼, 노력한 만큼, 눈물이 날 만큼”). Adjectives take “-ㄴ/은 만큼” (“중요한 만큼”). Real stems: “만들다 → 만든 만큼”, “알다 → 아는 만큼”, “먹다 → 먹은 만큼”. “만큼” is a separate word. It is a different thing from the particle “N만큼”, which is attached to a noun. The saying “아는 만큼 보인다” (you see as much as you know) is a set phrase.

examples.en: The results come in proportion to the effort.
You see as much as you know.
It was a view so beautiful it could bring tears.

examples.ko: 중요한 일인 만큼 신중하게 결정해야 합니다.
examples.en: Since it is an important matter, we must decide carefully.
You may eat as much as you want.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ수록” says that as one thing increases, so does another. “-는 만큼” says that the extent of the second matches the first.

pair.en: The more you try, the more your skill grows.
Your skill grows as much as you try.

compare.difference: In the “reason” use, “-는 만큼” gives a reason that suits the main clause; “-기 때문에” is a plain cause.

pair.en: Since you are busy, you have to look after your health.
Because I am busy, I cannot look after my health.

pitfalls.note: After a verb, “만큼” is a separate word, so there is a space.
pitfalls.en: You get as much as you put in effort.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-ㄴ”.
pitfalls.en: It sold as much as I made.

topik_tip: “-는 만큼” differs from the noun particle “N만큼”: the first follows a verb modifier and is spaced.

label: whereas, on the other hand
meaning_en: An expression that sets two facts against each other: “X, whereas Y; X, but on the other hand Y”. It suits advantages versus disadvantages and differences between people or periods.
usage: Verbs take “-는 반면(에)”, adjectives and “이다” take “-ㄴ/은 반면(에)” (“편리하다 → 편리한 반면”, “학생이다 → 학생인 반면”), past forms take “-었던 반면”. The “에” is optional. The two clauses must contrast, so the second often has an opposite quality or a downside. It is more written than “-지만”. “반면” is a separate word.

examples.en: The internet is convenient, but it also has many side effects.
Jisu is lively, whereas Seunggyu is quiet.

examples.ko: 이 일은 월급이 적은 반면에 보람이 크다.
examples.en: This job pays little, but it is very rewarding.

examples.ko: 여름에는 비가 많이 오는 반면 겨울에는 건조하다.
examples.en: It rains a lot in summer, whereas winter is dry.

examples.ko: 낮에는 따뜻했던 반면 밤에는 몹시 추웠다.
examples.en: It was warm during the day, but very cold at night.

compare.difference: “-지만” is the plain “but” and fits any contrast. “-는 반면” sets up a balanced, written contrast between two sides.

pair.en: The city is convenient, but prices are high.
The city is convenient, whereas prices are high.

compare.difference: “-는 대신에” adds compensation. “-는 반면” is neutral.

pair.en: The pay is low, whereas the reward is big.
The pay is low, but in return the reward is big.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은”, not “-는”.
pitfalls.en: The city is convenient, whereas prices are high.

pitfalls.note: The two parts must contrast; a plain cause or a sequence does not fit.
pitfalls.right: 낮에는 비가 오는 반면 밤에는 맑았다.
pitfalls.en: It rained during the day, whereas the night was clear.

topik_tip: Look for opposite qualities on either side of “반면”: that is the whole meaning.

label: it seems that (guess from evidence)
meaning_en: An expression for a guess based on what the speaker sees or hears: “it seems that ..., I guess ..., apparently ...”. It is used about a fact the speaker has not confirmed.
usage: Verbs, “있다/없다” and past stems take “-나 보다” (“오다 → 오나 보다”, “살다 → 사나 보다” with the ㄹ dropped, “듣다 → 듣나 보다”, “잤나 보다”); adjectives and “이다” normally take “-ㄴ가 보다” (“바쁜가 보다”, “학생인가 보다”). The speaker names a ground first or after (“불이 꺼져 있네. 아무도 없나 보다.”). It is for guesses about others or about a situation; a fact the speaker knows for certain does not take it. Polite: “-나 봐요”.

examples.ko: 밖에 비가 오나 보다. 사람들이 우산을 쓰고 있네.
examples.en: It seems to be raining outside. People are using umbrellas.

examples.ko: 민준이는 어제 잠을 못 잤나 보다. 눈이 빨개.
examples.en: Minjun seems not to have slept last night. Their eyes are red.

examples.ko: 불이 꺼져 있네. 아무도 없나 보다.
examples.en: The lights are off. Nobody seems to be there.

examples.ko: 이 집이 맛있나 보네요. 줄이 아주 길어요.
examples.en: This place must be good. The line is very long.

examples.ko: 지수가 요즘 바쁜가 보다. 연락이 없네.
examples.en: Jisu seems busy lately. There has been no word.

compare.difference: “-나 보다” rests on visible evidence of the present or the past. “-ㄹ 것 같다” is a broader guess and can look to the future.

pair.en: It seems to be raining.
It looks like it will rain.

compare.difference: “-나 보다” and “-는 모양이다” are close in meaning; “-는 모양이다” is a little more formal and fits written reports.

pair.en: Minjun seems to be sick.
Minjun seems to be sick.

pitfalls.note: It is a guess from evidence, so it does not fit what the speaker knows for certain.
pitfalls.en: Minjun seems to be Korean.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-나”.
pitfalls.en: They seem to be living in Seoul these days.

topik_tip: The guess from evidence (“나 보다”) and the guess about the future (“ㄹ 것 같다”) are different: look for a clue that has been seen.

label: should be ... (but); would have ...
meaning_en: An expression for a strong supposition followed by something connected: “it should be that ..., and/but ...”. It is also used for what would have happened, with “-았으면 ... -았을 텐데”, and for sympathy or worry about someone.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems: after a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ 텐데”, after other consonants “-을 텐데”. Real stems: “가다 → 갈 텐데”, “먹다 → 먹을 텐데”, “살다 → 살 텐데”, “만들다 → 만들 텐데”, “이다 → 일 텐데”, past “-았을/었을 텐데”. The speaker is fairly sure; the next clause gives advice, a question, a worry or a contrast. The polite ending is “-을 텐데요”. It is made of “-ㄹ 터이다” and “-ㄴ데”.

examples.ko: 밖이 추울 텐데 따뜻하게 입고 가세요.
examples.en: It must be cold outside, so dress warmly when you go.

examples.ko: 지금쯤 도착했을 텐데 왜 연락이 없지?
examples.en: They must have arrived by now, so why is there no word?
If you had told me beforehand, I would have helped.

examples.ko: 시험 때문에 많이 힘들 텐데 괜찮아요?
examples.en: You must be having a hard time because of the exam. Are you all right?
If we do not hurry, we will be late.

compare.difference: “-을 텐데” gives a supposition and the speech continues with a contrast or concern. “-을 테니” makes the supposition the reason for the main clause, often a request.

pair.en: It must be cold, so wear a coat.
It is going to be cold, so wear a coat.

compare.difference: “-겠-” with “-지” is a flat guess. “-을 텐데” opens a second clause or leaves the sentence hanging for a contrast, a worry or a request.

pair.en: They must have arrived by now.
They should have arrived by now.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem merges the ㄹ with “-ㄹ”: “살다” becomes “살 텐데”.
pitfalls.wrong: 지금 서울에 살을 텐데 연락해 볼까?
pitfalls.right: 지금 서울에 살 텐데 연락해 볼까?
pitfalls.en: They must be living in Seoul now, so shall I contact them?

topik_tip: It carries two moves: a firm supposition and a continuation (advice, worry or contrast).

label: in order to, for
meaning_en: An expression for a goal: “in order to do X” with verbs, and “for the sake of N” as “N을/를 위해(서)”. It is formal and common in writing and in speeches.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with no tense ending: “지키다 → 지키기 위해(서)”, “만들다 → 만들기 위해” (the ㄹ stays before “-기”). The forms “-기 위해서는” (to X, one must) and the modifier “-기 위한 N” (efforts for X) are frequent. The noun form is “N을/를 위해(서)” (“가족을 위해”). The main clause usually states an effort or a necessary condition.

examples.en: I exercise every day to stay healthy.
I came to Korea in order to learn Korean.
To pass, steady effort is needed.
I work hard for my family.
Efforts to protect the environment are needed.

compare.difference: “-으려고” is the everyday way to state a purpose; “-기 위해” is more formal and also forms the modifier “-기 위한”.

pair.en: I study in order to pass.
I study in order to pass.

compare.difference: “-으러” only works with “가다/오다” type verbs of motion. “-기 위해” works with any main verb.

pair.en: I came to study.
I came in order to study.

pitfalls.note: The first verb has no tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I studied in order to pass.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps the ㄹ before “-기”.
pitfalls.wrong: 맛있는 음식을 만드기 위해 재료를 골랐다.
pitfalls.right: 맛있는 음식을 만들기 위해 재료를 골랐다.
pitfalls.en: I chose the ingredients to make tasty food.

topik_tip: The list's related forms “-기 위해서, -기 위한, N을 위해” are the same expression in different shapes.

label: as long as it isn't N
meaning_en: An expression meaning “if only it were not N” or “as long as it is not N”: N is the one obstacle or exception, and anything else is fine. It is also used for “if it were not for N, I would ...”.
usage: It attaches to a noun: “N만 아니면”. The main clause says what would then follow: a counterfactual (“-ㄹ 텐데, -았을 텐데”) or a statement that all else is acceptable (“괜찮다, 돼요, 상관없다”). With a clause instead of a noun the shape is “-지만 않으면” (“비가 오지만 않으면”). The spaced “아니면” is the “-이/가 아니다” + “-면”.

examples.en: If it were not for the rain, we would go on the picnic.

examples.ko: 시험만 아니면 같이 여행 갈 수 있을 텐데.
examples.en: If it were not for the exam, I could go on a trip with you.

examples.ko: 매운 음식만 아니면 뭐든지 잘 먹어요.
examples.en: I eat anything well, as long as it is not spicy food.
I can forgive anything as long as it is not a lie.
Any day is fine, as long as it is not Monday.

compare.difference: “N이 아니면” just says “if it is not N”. “N만 아니면” singles out N as the only obstacle.

pair.en: Anything but Monday is fine.
If it is not Monday, it is fine.

compare.difference: “비만 아니면” is a noun obstacle. With a clause, “-지만 않으면” does the same job.

pair.en: I will go, rain permitting.
I will go as long as it does not rain.

pitfalls.note: After a clause, use “-지만 않으면”; “만 아니면” follows a noun.
pitfalls.wrong: 비가 오는 만 아니면 소풍을 갈 텐데.
pitfalls.right: 비가 오지만 않으면 소풍을 갈 텐데.
pitfalls.en: As long as it does not rain, we would go on the picnic.

topik_tip: Read it as “only X stands in the way”. The main clause often has “-ㄹ 텐데” or “괜찮다”.

label: must not
meaning_en: An expression for a prohibition or a limit: “you must not X, X is not allowed”. It can also say that a state is not acceptable (“너무 비싸면 안 된다”).
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-면 안 되다”, after other consonants “-으면 안 되다”; it attaches to verbs, adjectives and “이다”. Real stems: “피우다 → 피우면”, “놀다 → 놀면”, “먹다 → 먹으면”, “눕다 → 누우면” (ㅂ-irregular), “걷다 → 걸으면”. The spoken form is “안 돼요”; “되어” contracts to “돼”, so it is never “안 되요”. The opposite pattern is “-으면 되다” (it is enough to X), and the pattern for permission is “-어도 되다”.

examples.ko: 도서관에서는 큰 소리로 말하면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not talk loudly in the library.
