examples.ko: 수업 시간에 휴대전화를 보면 안 되니까 가방에 넣어 두세요.
examples.en: You must not look at your phone during class, so put it in your bag.

examples.ko: 이 약은 술과 함께 먹으면 안 되므로 주의하십시오.
examples.en: This medicine must not be taken together with alcohol, so please be careful.

examples.ko: 아무리 화가 나도 사람을 때리면 안 돼.
examples.en: No matter how angry you are, you must not hit people.
You must not lie, of course.

compare.difference: “-으면 안 되다” states a rule; “-지 마세요” is a direct request not to do it.

pair.en: You must not smoke here.
Please do not smoke here.

compare.difference: “-으면 되다” says that X is enough; “-으면 안 되다” says that X is not allowed.

pair.en: It is fine to wait here.
You must not wait here.

pitfalls.note: “되어” contracts to “돼”: the spoken form is “안 돼요”.
pitfalls.en: You must not swim here.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular verb turns ㅂ into “우”.
pitfalls.en: You must not lie down during class.

topik_tip: Spelling “안 돼요” (not “안 되요”) and the ㅂ-irregular “누우면” are the points that exams like.

label: I hope that; it would be nice if
meaning_en: An expression for a hope or wish: “I hope (that) ..., I wish ..., it would be nice if ...”. It is also a polite way of asking someone for something (“조용히 해 주면 좋겠어요”).
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-면 좋겠다”, after other consonants “-으면 좋겠다”; it attaches to verbs, adjectives and “이다”. The past-looking “-았/었으면 좋겠다” is just as common and adds a wishful, less certain tone (“날씨가 맑았으면 좋겠어요”). Real stems: “살다 → 살면”, “덥다 → 더우면”, “듣다 → 들으면”. The wished-for situation is in the first clause, and the subject may be the speaker, the listener or a third party. A request form: “-어 주면 좋겠다”.

examples.en: I hope the weather is clear tomorrow.
I hope I pass this exam.
I would appreciate it if you could be a bit quieter.

examples.ko: 방학에 가족과 함께 여행을 가면 좋겠다.
examples.en: It would be nice to go on a trip with the family during the vacation.
I wish I were just a little taller.

compare.difference: “-고 싶다” is the speaker wanting to do something. “-으면 좋겠다” wishes for a situation and can include others or things beyond one's control.

pair.en: I want to leave work early.
It would be nice to leave work early.

compare.difference: “-았으면 하다” is a near-synonym that sounds more reserved or formal.

pair.en: I hope the rain stops.
I hope the rain stops.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우”.
pitfalls.en: I hope it is a bit less cold.

pitfalls.note: “-고 싶다” is for one's own wish to do something; a hoped-for situation takes “-으면 좋겠다”.
pitfalls.en: I hope the rain stops.

topik_tip: A hope about a situation takes “-으면 좋겠다”; one's own desire to do something takes “-고 싶다”.

label: gradually keep on (toward the future)
meaning_en: An expression for a change or an action that continues step by step from now on: “gradually ..., keep on ...-ing”. It looks forward from the present, often with “점점, 조금씩, 차츰”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with “-아/어” and the helper “가다”: “늘다 → 늘어 가다”, “깊다 → 깊어 가다”, “익다 → 익어 가다”, “밝다 → 밝아 가다”, “줄다 → 줄어 가다”. It goes with verbs of change or with an action that continues: “해결해 가다, 배워 가다, 만들어 가다”. The “-어 오다” counterpart looks back from now (“해 왔다”). The same words can also mean “do X and go” (“사 가다”, “입고 가다” with “-고”), so context matters.

examples.en: Autumn is deepening.

examples.ko: 공부를 하다 보니 한국어 실력이 조금씩 늘어 가요.
examples.en: As I keep studying, my Korean is gradually improving.
The day was gradually dawning.
The kimchi is ripening nicely.

examples.ko: 어려운 일도 하나씩 풀어 가면 된다.
examples.en: Even a hard task is fine if you untangle it one piece at a time.

compare.difference: “-어 가다” looks forward from now (what will go on); “-어 오다” looks back (what has gone on up to now).

pair.en: I will keep living hard from now on.
I have lived hard up to now.

compare.difference: “-고 있다” says the action is in progress now; “-어 간다” adds that it keeps moving on gradually.

pair.en: My skills are improving.
My skills are improving gradually.

pitfalls.note: The helper needs “-아/어”; with “-고” it means “do X and then go”.
pitfalls.en: My skills are gradually improving.

topik_tip: Pair the two: “-어 가다” moves toward the future, “-어 오다” comes from the past up to now.

label: spoken “and then / so” (result continues)
meaning_en: A spoken connective that links an action to what follows with its result still in effect: “did X, and (with that) ...”. It also gives a cause in casual talk (“because ...”) and means “holding/keeping” with “있다”. It is close to “-어서”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems with “-아/어”: “먹다 → 먹어 가지고”, “잡다 → 잡아 가지고”, “얻다 → 얻어 가지고”, “사다 → 사 가지고”; often shortened to “-어 갖고”. The first verb takes no tense ending (“먹었어 가지고” is wrong). Three uses: a sequence with carried result (“사 가지고 오다”), a cause (“너무 많이 먹어 가지고 배가 아프다”) and a continuing state (“자리를 잡아 가지고 있다”). It is for conversation, not for formal writing.

examples.ko: 너무 많이 먹어 가지고 배가 아파요.
examples.en: I ate too much, so my stomach hurts.

examples.ko: 생선을 잡아 가지고 바로 구워 먹었다.
examples.en: We caught fish and grilled and ate them right away.

examples.ko: 친구한테 돈을 얻어 가지고 학원비를 냈다.
examples.en: I got some money from a friend and paid the tuition.

examples.ko: 내가 먼저 가서 자리를 잡아 가지고 있을게.
examples.en: I will go first and keep the seats.
I will buy some bread and bring it along.

compare.difference: In a cause or a sequence “-어 가지고” and “-어서” can swap. “-어 가지고” is colloquial; “-어서” is neutral and also used in writing.

pair.ko: 너무 많이 먹어 가지고 배가 아파요.
pair.en: I ate too much, so my stomach hurts.
I ate too much, so my stomach hurts.

compare.difference: “-어다가” says the object is carried from one place to another. “-어 가지고” can do the same with “오다/가다” and is more spoken.

pair.en: I bought bread and brought it to give.
I bought bread, came with it and gave it.

pitfalls.note: The first verb takes no tense ending.
pitfalls.wrong: 너무 많이 먹었어 가지고 배가 아파요.
pitfalls.right: 너무 많이 먹어 가지고 배가 아파요.
pitfalls.en: I ate too much, so my stomach hurts.

topik_tip: It is a spoken pattern; the formal written equivalent is “-어서” or “-고”.

label: do X and leave it done
meaning_en: An expression for doing something and leaving the result in place, often as preparation: “leave ... open”, “have ... ready”, “write down”. The finished state stays as it is.
usage: It attaches to transitive verb stems with “-아/어”: “열다 → 열어 놓다”, “닫다 → 닫아 놓다”, “적다 → 적어 놓다”, “만들다 → 만들어 놓다”, “넣다 → 넣어 놓다”; with “하다” it is “해 놓다”. The object of the first verb carries on the stated state (“창문을 열어 놓았다”). It is close to “-어 두다”, and the two swap in many sentences. The result-state counterpart without an agent is “-어 있다” (“창문이 열려 있다”).

examples.en: It was hot, so I slept with the window left open.

examples.ko: 손님이 오기 전에 음식을 미리 만들어 놓았다.
examples.en: I made the food in advance, before the guests came.

examples.ko: 내일 입을 옷을 침대 위에 꺼내 놓았다.
examples.en: I took out the clothes to wear tomorrow and laid them on the bed.

examples.ko: 중요한 내용은 공책에 적어 놓으면 잊어버리지 않는다.
examples.en: If you write down the important content in a notebook, you will not forget it.

examples.ko: 숙제를 다 해 놓고 놀러 갔다.
examples.en: I finished all my homework and went out to play.

compare.difference: The two are near-synonyms, and in many sentences either works (“적어 놓다 / 적어 두다”). “-어 두다” leans toward keeping something for later, “-어 놓다” toward leaving it done.

pair.en: I wrote it down in a notebook.
I wrote it down in a notebook.

compare.difference: “-어 놓다” has an agent who did the action; “-어 있다” describes only the resulting state.

pair.en: I left the window open.
The window is open.

pitfalls.note: “-어 놓다” needs a transitive verb with an object; the object takes “을/를”.
pitfalls.en: I left the window open.

pitfalls.note: The first verb takes no tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I did my homework and went out to play.

topik_tip: Contrast the agent version “-어 놓다” with the state version “-어 있다”: “열어 놓았다” and “열려 있다”.

label: do X and keep it for later
meaning_en: An expression for doing something and keeping the result for later use, or preparing in advance: “write down, put away, keep in mind”. It is common with “알아 두다” (to keep in mind).
usage: It attaches to transitive verb stems with “-아/어”: “적다 → 적어 두다”, “넣다 → 넣어 두다”, “닫다 → 닫아 두다”, “알다 → 알아 두다”, “맡다 → 맡아 두다”, “사다 → 사 두다”. With “알다” the idiom is “알아 두세요” (keep this in mind), where “알아 놓다” is not the usual form. In most other cases “-어 놓다” and “-어 두다” can be exchanged. A habit is “미리 -어 두다” (do it beforehand).

examples.en: I wrote the appointment time on the calendar.

examples.ko: 이 단어는 시험에 자주 나오니까 잘 알아 두세요.
examples.en: This word comes up often in exams, so keep it in mind.

examples.ko: 비가 올지 몰라서 우산을 가방에 넣어 두었다.
examples.en: It might rain, so I put an umbrella in my bag.

examples.ko: 여행 가기 전에 표를 미리 사 두는 게 좋다.
examples.en: It is good to buy the tickets in advance before traveling.

examples.ko: 아이가 깰까 봐 방문을 닫아 두었다.
examples.en: I closed the room door so as not to wake the child.

compare.difference: The two are interchangeable in many sentences, but “알아 두다” (keep in mind) is the normal idiom, and “-어 놓다” also suits finishing something so that it is done.

pair.en: Keep this in mind.
I finished all my homework.

pitfalls.note: The first verb takes no tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I wrote it down in a notebook.

topik_tip: “알아 두세요” (keep this in mind) is a set formula in notices and listening items.

label: do for someone senior (honorific “-어 주다”)
meaning_en: An honorific helper meaning “do (something) for a person one respects”. It is the humble counterpart of “-어 주다”, with the beneficiary elevated: “I do it for you/for the elder”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with “-아/어”: “읽다 → 읽어 드리다”, “닦다 → 닦아 드리다”, “찾다 → 찾아 드리다”, “돕다 → 도와 드리다” (ㅂ-irregular), “끓이다 → 끓여 드리다”. The one who does is the speaker (or someone on the speaker's side), and the one who benefits is the person to be honoured. Typical frames: “-어 드릴게요, -어 드릴까요?, -어 드리겠습니다”. If the honoured person is the doer, the verb is “-어 주시다”. For equals and juniors the pattern is “-어 주다”.

examples.en: I read a storybook to my grandmother.
That looks heavy; let me carry it for you.
Shall I take a photo for you, if you would like?
I made some warm tea for the guest.
How may I help you?

compare.difference: “-어 드리다” is for the one you honour; “-어 주다” is for friends, children and juniors.

pair.en: I read a book to my grandmother.
I read a book to my younger sibling.

compare.difference: The direction flips: with “-어 드리다” you serve the elder; with “-어 주시다” the elder does something for you.

pair.en: I read a book to my teacher.
My teacher read a book to me.

pitfalls.note: The beneficiary has to be someone to honour; for a friend or younger person use “-어 주다”.
pitfalls.en: I took a photo for my grandmother.

pitfalls.note: When the honoured person does the action, “-어 주시다” is used instead.
pitfalls.en: My teacher read the book for me.

topik_tip: Check the direction: speaker to honoured person is “-어 드리다”; honoured person to speaker is “-어 주시다”.

label: I'd better; I have to (decision)
meaning_en: An ending of resolve or conclusion: “I will have to, I had better, I should (from now)”. The speaker reaches the decision from a situation they have just noticed. It also marks a guess that something looks necessary.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems with “-아/어” plus “-야겠-” and then a sentence ending: “먹다 → 먹어야겠다”, “찾다 → 찾아야겠다”, “듣다 → 들어야겠다” (ㄷ-irregular), “돕다 → 도와야겠다” (ㅂ-irregular), “하다 → 해야겠다”. It is mainly a first-person decision (statement) or a question to the listener (“-어야겠어요?”). For someone else it gives an opinion (“너도 가야겠다”). Related: “-어야지” as a resolution, “-어야 하다” as a general duty.

examples.en: I am so hungry. I had better eat something.

examples.ko: 모르는 단어가 너무 많네. 사전을 찾아야겠다.
examples.en: There are so many words I do not know. I had better look in the dictionary.
I have to get an apology from that person in person.
I cannot go on like this. I have to pull myself together.

examples.ko: 비가 올 것 같으니까 우산을 가져가야겠어요.
examples.en: It looks like rain, so I will take an umbrella.

compare.difference: “-어야 하다” states an obligation in general. “-어야겠-” is the speaker's own conclusion or decision at this moment.

pair.en: I have to go now.
I will have to go now.

compare.difference: As a resolution to oneself the two are near-synonyms. “-어야겠-” has a more deliberate sound as a conclusion.

pair.en: I should eat now.
I had better eat now.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular stem turns ㄷ into ㄹ before “-어”.
pitfalls.en: I have to take this lecture.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular stem becomes “와/워” plus the ending.
pitfalls.en: I have to help my friend.

topik_tip: It is a decision made now; a duty stated in general is “-어야 하다”.

label: become; be done (by itself)
meaning_en: An expression with two uses: with an adjective it means “become, get ...” (a change of state), and with a transitive verb it means “be done, come to be done”, often by someone or something unspecified.
usage: It attaches to stems with “-아/어”: “좋다 → 좋아지다”, “높다 → 높아지다”, “예쁘다 → 예뻐지다” (ㅡ drops), “춥다 → 추워지다” (ㅂ-irregular), “깨끗하다 → 깨끗해지다”; with verbs “만들다 → 만들어지다”, “이루다 → 이루어지다”, “믿다 → 믿어지다”. Action verbs in “-하다” form the passive with “-되다” (“실행되다”), not “-해지다”. The form “믿어지지 않는다” (hard to believe) is a set expression. Do not double a passive: “열리다” already means “be opened”.

examples.ko: 운동을 시작한 뒤로 건강이 많이 좋아졌어요.
examples.en: Since I started exercising, my health has improved a lot.
This furniture is made of wood.
When the sun set, the sky gradually grew dark.
I cannot bring myself to believe that news.
After long effort, the dream came true.

compare.difference: “-어지다” is a gradual change of a state. “-게 되다” is a change in circumstance or a result that comes about.

pair.en: Korean has become easier.
I have come to study Korean.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우”: “춥다” becomes “추워지다”.
pitfalls.en: The weather gradually got colder.

pitfalls.note: The ending attaches to the stem; it is not a separate “게”.
pitfalls.en: The room became clean.

topik_tip: With an adjective it is “become”; with a verb it is “be done”: the stem type tells you which.

label: about, regarding
meaning_en: A formal expression marking a topic: “about, concerning”. The topics of thinking, saying, learning and researching take it. In speech it is “에 대해(서)”, and before a noun “에 대한 N”.
usage: It attaches to a noun: “환경에 대하여 / 환경에 대해(서)”. The modifier form is “N에 대한 + noun” (“환경에 대한 관심”). The predicate is a verb of thought or communication: “이야기하다, 생각하다, 말하다, 조사하다, 배우다, 질문하다, 설명하다”. With a verb, “에 대한” cannot be used; it is “에 대해”. “에 대해서는” singles out the topic (“그 일에 대해서는 말할 수 없다”).

examples.ko: 오늘은 한국의 전통 문화에 대하여 이야기하겠습니다.
examples.en: Today I will talk about Korea's traditional culture.
What do you think about this problem?

examples.ko: 환경 보호에 대한 관심이 높아지고 있다.
examples.en: Interest in protecting the environment is growing.

examples.ko: 지수는 한국 역사에 대해서 공부하고 있다.
examples.en: Jisu is studying Korean history.

examples.ko: 그 사건에 대해서는 말씀드릴 수 없습니다.
examples.en: I cannot say anything about that incident.

compare.difference: “친구에 대해” makes the friend the topic; “친구에게” makes the friend the one spoken to.

pair.en: I talked about my friend.
I told my friend.

compare.difference: “에 대하여” and “에 관하여” are near-synonyms; both mean “about, concerning”.

pair.en: We discussed the environment.
We discussed the environment.

pitfalls.note: “에 대한” modifies a noun; with a verb, use “에 대해”.
pitfalls.en: I talked about Korean culture.

topik_tip: The three shapes “에 대하여 / 에 대해서 / 에 대한” are one expression; “에 대한” goes before a noun.

label: I will ..., so; it will ..., so
meaning_en: A connective expression for the speaker's intention or supposition as the ground of what follows: “I will do X, so (you) ...” or “it will be X, so ...”. The main clause is normally a request, command or suggestion.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ 테니”, after other consonants “-을 테니”: “가다 → 갈 테니”, “먹다 → 먹을 테니”, “놀다 → 놀 테니”, “만들다 → 만들 테니”, past “-았을 테니”. With a first-person subject it expresses a promise or an intention (“내가 갈 테니 기다려”); otherwise it is a prediction (“추울 테니 코트를 입어”). “-을 테니까” is the same with more stress, and the sentence-ending counterpart of the promise is “-을게”.

examples.ko: 내가 먼저 갈 테니 천천히 와.
examples.en: I will go first, so come slowly.

examples.ko: 설거지는 제가 할 테니 쉬고 계세요.
examples.en: I will do the dishes, so please take a rest.

examples.ko: 밖이 추울 테니 두꺼운 옷을 입으세요.
examples.en: It will be cold outside, so wear thick clothes.

examples.ko: 곧 비가 올 테니 우산을 가져가세요.
examples.en: It will rain soon, so take an umbrella.
You must have been tired, so rest early today.

compare.difference: “-을게” closes the sentence as a promise. “-을 테니” connects the promise to the next clause.

pair.en: I will do the dishes. You rest.
I will do the dishes, so you rest.

compare.difference: “-을 테니” makes the supposition the ground of a request; “-을 텐데” leaves the sentence open for a contrast or worry.

pair.en: It will be cold, so wear a coat.
It must be cold; wear a coat.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem merges the ㄹ with “-ㄹ”: “놀다” becomes “놀 테니”.
pitfalls.en: I will play with the child, so please rest.

pitfalls.note: The main clause is a request, command or suggestion, not a plain past statement.
pitfalls.en: I will do it, so please rest.

topik_tip: The promise sense (“내가 -ㄹ 테니”) and the supposition sense are both tested: see who the subject is.

label: have been doing up to now
meaning_en: An expression for an action or state that has continued from the past up to the present: “have been X-ing all along, have kept X-ing”. It looks back from now, often with “지금까지, 오랫동안, 예전부터”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with “-아/어”: “믿다 → 믿어 오다”, “살다 → 살아 오다”, “이어지다 → 이어져 오다”, “쌓다 → 쌓아 오다”, “하다 → 해 오다”. It is usually in the past (“-어 왔다”) or in a modifier (“-어 온”). The same form can mean “do X and come” (“사 오다”). Its counterpart “-어 가다” goes forward into the future.

examples.ko: 이 가게는 삼십 년 동안 같은 맛을 이어 오고 있다.
examples.en: This shop has kept the same taste for thirty years.
We have trusted each other for a long time.
My grandfather has lived in poverty all his life.

examples.ko: 지금까지 열심히 노력해 왔으니 이번에는 꼭 될 거야.
examples.en: You have been trying hard until now, so it will surely work this time.

examples.ko: 대대로 같은 방식으로 농사를 지어 오는 마을이다.
examples.en: It is a village that has farmed in the same way for generations.

compare.difference: “-어 오다” looks back from the present; “-어 가다” goes on toward the future.

pair.en: I have been doing it hard until now.
I will keep doing it hard from now on.

compare.difference: “-고 있다” is in progress now; “-어 오다” covers the whole stretch up to now.

pair.en: I am doing this work.
I have been doing this work.

pitfalls.note: It looks back from now; for the future, use “-어 가다”.
pitfalls.en: I will keep doing it hard from now on.

topik_tip: “지금까지” in a sentence points to “-어 오다”, and “앞으로” to “-어 가다”.

label: “oh, not really” (modest denial); X, yes, but
meaning_en: An ending (often “-기는요/-긴요”) used to gently deny or push back a compliment or a statement by repeating its stem: “잘하기는요” (do well? not really). Inside a sentence, “-기는 하다” grants a point and then adds a “but”.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems (“잘하다 → 잘하기는요”, “예쁘다 → 예쁘기는요”, “고맙다 → 고맙기는요”, “예술가이다 → 예술가이기는요”). Shortened to “-긴(요)”. The stem repeats the word of the other person. The reply is modest and often followed by a reason. In the “-기는 하다” frame (“재미있기는 한데 길어요”) the speaker admits something and then adds a reservation. The two uses share the same form.

examples.en: Not really. I still have a long way to go.
No need to thank me. It is only what I should do.
Pretty? Not really. It is so cramped that it is inconvenient.

examples.ko: 그 영화는 재미있기는 한데 너무 길어요.
examples.en: That movie is interesting, to be sure, but it is too long.
I did eat it, but I could not tell the taste.

compare.difference: “-기는 하지만” first concedes the point; “-지만” alone is a plain contrast.

pair.en: It is interesting, all right, but long.
It is interesting but long.

compare.difference: “-기는요” echoes the other person's word; “아니에요” is a plain “no”.

pair.en: You do well. — Not really.
You do well. — No.

pitfalls.note: It attaches to the bare stem, not to a full sentence ending.
pitfalls.en: Not really, I don't do well.

topik_tip: “-기는요” (modest denial) and “-기는 하다” (concession) are the two shapes of this form.
